items.title: Abnormal starts

numbers.label: Abort if ITT likely to exceed
Abort if ITT likely to remain
Abort if no ITT rise within
BATT BUS warning may precede MFD failure at
Auto-abort if N1 acceleration to idle

items.lede: In the AUTO start mode, if a no start is detected or if a hung or hot start is projected, the PMU should terminate the start sequence. You should always be prepared to manually abort a start if the PMU fails to do its job and an abort is warranted.

items.title: Aborted takeoff
items.lede: An aborted takeoff may be required during any takeoff. Any situation which appears abnormal or unsafe during takeoff shall necessitate an abort. If it becomes necessary to abort the takeoff, concentrate on maintaining aircraft control, specifically directional control, while stopping the aircraft on the remaining runway.

items.title: Accelerated stall

numbers.label: Do not sustain heavy buffet above

items.lede: Turning flight and maneuvers produce an effect on stall speed which is similar to the effect of weight, and the stalling speed of an airplane is higher in a level turn than in straight and level flight. Low indicated airspeed is not necessary to produce a stall, since the pilot can demand more lift than the wing can generate, causing an excessive angle of attack at any speed. An accelerated stall induced by a turning entry and increased G is preceded by pronounced airframe buffet before the stall is reached, and during a turning entry the stall is characterized by a moderately abrupt lateral roll-off.

items.title: Acceleration limitations
items.lede: The operating flight strengths are shown in NATOPS Figure 5-4, as symmetric and asymmetric (rolling G's) limits for the clean configuration and with gear and/or flaps extended. Zero G is limited to 5 seconds maximum, and negative G operation, including inverted, is limited to 60 seconds.

items.title: Aerobatic maneuvers

references.loc: §901 — Rules and Precautions for Aerobatic Flight
§902 — Section Lines and Ground Reference Points

items.lede: Aerobatics is any intentional maneuver involving an abrupt change in aircraft’s attitude, intentionally performed spins, or other maneuvers requiring pitch/dive angles greater than 45°, bank angles greater than 60°, or accelerations greater than two G’s. Start your aerobatic maneuvers from an altitude which will permit a complete maneuver and a return to straight and level flight at or above 6000 feet AGL.

items.title: Aileron roll
items.lede: The Aileron Roll is a 360° roll about the longitudinal axis of the aircraft. The maneuver is complete when the wings are parallel to the horizon. When performing the maneuver make your control inputs smooth, brisk and positive.

items.title: Airborne-damaged aircraft

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Controllability Check (Structural Damage/Flight Control Malfunction)

items.lede: If a bird strike, structural damage, or a flight control malfunction occurs or is suspected in flight, a decision to abandon the aircraft or attempt a landing must be made. A mid-air collision is an inherent risk when flying formation. Mid-air collisions can be either minimal or catastrophic and can be within the section or external to the flight.

items.title: Aircraft and cockpit lighting
items.lede: The aircraft is equipped with exterior lighting that meets the requirements for operation of the aircraft during night and low light conditions, and all instruments, control panels, and displays in both cockpits are lighted for operation during night or reduced light conditions. The landing light and the taxi light illuminate only when all three gear are down and locked. If NIGHT mode is selected in either cockpit, the MFDs and UFCPs in the whole aircraft are placed into the night mode.

items.title: Aircraft departs prepared surface

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground
Ch. 3 — Landing With Blown Main Tire

items.lede: If it appears likely that the aircraft will depart the prepared surface, execute the Emergency Engine Shutdown On The Ground procedure.

items.title: Aircraft discrepancy reporting

references.loc: §3.12 — Degraded Integrated Avionics Computer Mitigation Procedures
§3.2 — Actual Emergencies and Precautionary Emergency Landings

items.lede: A flight that executes an emergency procedure, that is terminated by a malfunction requiring a precautionary emergency landing, or that is terminated by an aircrew illness requiring medical attention is reported to the ODO, who ensures the CO, XO, OPSO, Safety Officer and the TW-4 Command Duty Officer are notified. VT-27 and VT-28 each state that trigger in their own terms, and each requires a different report afterwards.

items.title: Aircraft issue

references.loc: §3.12 — Degraded Integrated Avionics Computer Mitigation Procedures

items.lede: Aircrew verify side number and parking spot in maintenance control and verbally confirm with the other crew member before opening the canopy. A degraded integrated avionics computer decides whether the aircraft is taken at all.

items.title: Airfield and runway lighting

references.loc: Section B §7 — Pilot Control of Airport Lighting
Section B §6 — Wave-Off Lighting at USN/USMC Airports

items.lede: Blue lights mark all taxiways, white lights mark the boundaries of the duty runway, green lights mark the threshold of the duty runway, and red lights mark all obstructions on the airfield.

items.title: Airspace classification

numbers.label: Victor airways
numbers.value: 1200 feet AGL to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL

items.lede: The AIM defines controlled airspace as "a generic term that covers the different classifications of airspace (Class A, B, C, D, and E) and defined dimensions within which air traffic control service is provided to IFR and VFR flights in accordance with the airspace classification." Safety, users' needs, and volume of flight operations are some of the factors considered in the designation of controlled airspace. When flying a visual navigation route under VFR, visibility and cloud clearance requirements are different in controlled and uncontrolled airspace.

items.title: Airspeed changes
items.lede: Smooth, controlled, deliberate change of airspeed is an integral part of instrument flying. Change airspeed while maintaining heading and altitude. Power is used to initiate the change, and at the completion of the change power is set to maintain the new airspeed. The aircraft should be trimmed during airspeed changes and then fine-tuned once the target airspeed is achieved. This maneuver is normally practiced between 150 and 200 KIAS, and the Power-Attitude-Trim principle applies.

items.title: Airway navigation
items.lede: An intersection is a navigational fix that can be defined in the T-6B using VOR/DME, VOR only, or GPS. When referencing two or more NAVAIDs, the primary NAVAID is the one used to navigate a track to the intersection, and a secondary NAVAID is one that provides a crosscut to identify the intersection along the primary track. When the secondary is tuned depends on which of the three defines the fix. Be aware of which VORs along your route have voice capability in the event you lose both your UHF and VHF radios.

items.title: Aldis lamp signals

references.loc: Appendix B — Local VFR NORDO Procedures

items.lede: Aircraft with radio failure should observe the tower for light signals to obtain clearance to taxi, takeoff, land, etc. Acknowledge signals in the daytime by movement of ailerons or rudder on the ground and by rocking wings in the air. Acknowledge signals at night by flashing aircraft lights.

items.title: Alternate filing minimums
items.lede: Flight plans shall be filed based on the actual weather at the point of departure at the time of clearance, the existing and forecast weather for the entire route of flight, and destination and alternate forecasts for a period 1 hour before ETA until 1 hour after ETA. IFR flight plans may be filed for a destination at which the forecasted weather is below the appropriate minimums provided a suitable alternate airfield is forecast to have at least 3,000-foot ceiling and 3-statute-mile visibility during that period.

items.title: Anti-spin recovery procedures

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight

items.lede: Recover from a steady state spin by using NATOPS erect spin recovery procedures. Apply full rudder opposite to the direction of turn needle, follow immediately with smooth, positive forward stick to a position forward of neutral, and do not use ailerons.

items.title: AOA approach
items.lede: The AOA approach is a descending 180° balanced turn to final followed by a normal flared landing. During the approach, the optimum AOA is maintained by controlling nose/pitch attitude and rate of descent is controlled by power adjustment. The purpose of the AOA approach is to fly the aircraft as slow and as safe as possible.

items.title: Approach maneuver
items.lede: In addition to developing basic airwork scan and trim skills, the Approach Pattern incorporates many of the basic skill sets required during execution of a Low Altitude Instrument Approach from over a NAVAID. It runs two minutes of timing, a 210° turn, three 1000 foot descents, two of them at 120 KIAS in the Basic Approach Configuration, and a missed approach.

items.title: Arc-radial intercepts
items.lede: Turn off an arc to establish the aircraft on a radial, inbound or outbound, to the NAVAID. During some approaches, missed approaches and departure procedures you will be required to fly an arc and then intercept a radial from that arc. In this situation you need to calculate a lead radial at which to start your turn off the arc to intercept the radial.

items.title: Arcing approach

numbers.label: Charted lead radial, arc over 90° to course

items.lede: An arcing approach makes use of an arcing maneuver to position the aircraft inbound on an intermediate or final approach course. Arcing approaches are normally identified by VOR/DME or TACAN in the approach plate margin, indicating DME is required.

items.title: Arcing
items.lede: Arcing is defined as flying at a constant distance from a NAVAID by referencing DME from that station. Arcing about a NAVAID may be required to comply with an ATC clearance and is an integral part of many approaches, departure procedures, and arrivals. In practice, you do not actually fly a perfect arc, but by varying AOB and heading, a close approximation of an arc can be achieved.

items.title: Area and sun management
items.lede: The Formation Lead will keep the flight within the proper operating area and clear of clouds and other aircraft. As Lead, it is important to take the sun into consideration while maneuvering the flight. During early morning flights and late afternoon flights, particularly in the winter months, the sun is lower in the sky and will be more of a factor.

items.title: ASR approach

references.loc: §907 — Airport Surveillance Approach (ASR) and PAR Without Glideslope (PAR W/O GS)
§5.3.5.5 — Final Approach Abnormalities During Radar Approaches

items.lede: During the ASR approach, the controller utilizes an airport surveillance radar system to transition the aircraft to the runway environment. This controller can only provide course and range information. Because no glideslope information is available, it constitutes a non-precision approach.

items.title: Avionics malfunctions

references.loc: Ch. 3 — MFD Failure or Avionics Bus Failure
Ch. 3 — Backup Flight Instrument Display Failure

items.lede: During all electronic display failures, the pilot should confirm indications in both cockpits (if occupied), reference alternate data sources or the backup instruments as applicable, and check applicable circuit breakers. The term reset is used to describe the action of resetting a circuit breaker that is already open. The pilot should assess the severity of the emergency and equipment lost prior to resetting or opening any circuit breaker.

items.title: Barrel roll

references.loc: §902 — Section Lines and Ground Reference Points

items.lede: A Barrel Roll is a maneuver in which the aircraft is rolled 360° about an imaginary point which bears 45° off the nose of the aircraft. Definite seat pressure should be felt throughout the roll. Practice in both directions.

items.title: BASH

numbers.label: Strikes at or below 3,000 feet AGL

references.loc: Ch. 1 §9 — Bird Aircraft Strike Hazard (BASH) Program
§7-5-4 — Reporting Bird and Other Wildlife Activities
§7-5-5 — Pilot Advisories on Bird and Other Wildlife Hazards

items.lede: Bird strike risk increases because of bird migration during the months of March through April, and August through November. The most serious strikes are those involving ingestion into an engine (turboprops and turbine jet engines) or windshield strikes. In addition to pre-flight planning, CTW-4 ACs must, to the maximum extent practicable, inform ATC, the RDO, and/or other CTW-4 aircraft (on base frequencies) of the presence of birds that may pose a threat to operations.

items.title: Basic air work
items.lede: Basic Air Work is one of the Universally Graded Items, graded on all complete syllabus events. The behavior statement is to establish and maintain desired altitude, airspeed and heading during flight.

items.title: Basic transitions
items.lede: Basic transitions are used to initiate and/or level off from a climb or descent. The four basic transitions are climb-to-cruise, cruise-to-climb, cruise-to-descent, and descent-to-cruise. Use the P.A.T. principle to make all transitions.

items.title: Battery and generator failure
items.lede: This checklist assumes that the generator has failed and the main battery is totally depleted. The only operative instruments with auxiliary battery power will be the backup flight instrument, fire detection system (FIRE 1 only), IRU, and VHF radio (tuning provided by the standby VHF control head).

items.title: Battery bus light during start
items.lede: The engine start should be aborted manually if the red BATT BUS warning message illuminates during the start sequence.

items.title: BFI approach
items.lede: Maneuver the aircraft by means of the backup flight instrument only. With a loss of inputs from the Air Data Computer, the Internal Reference Unit, or in the event of a dual Integrated Avionics Computer failure with total loss of all MFDs, the Primary Flight Display may be lost or rendered unusable; however, flight may be continued and aircraft attitude controlled by referring to the BFI.

items.title: Backup flight instrument
items.lede: The backup flight instrument is located in the upper right side of the instrument panel in each cockpit and provides attitude, altitude, airspeed, heading and vertical velocity. This instrument provides backup indications in the event of failure of the electronic flight instrumentation system or the aircraft electrical system.

items.title: Blind procedures
items.lede: Blind is the term used to communicate that visual contact is lost with a member of the formation while maneuvering in VMC. In the event Wing loses sight of Lead in VMC, Wing will immediately call "(TAC call sign), blind, (altitude)". The visual aircraft has de-confliction responsibility.

items.title: Blindfold cockpit check
items.lede: Blindfold cockpit check is the Special Syllabus Requirement on FAM2101: the SNA demonstrates a safe knowledge of location of eleven cockpit controls. Special Syllabus Requirements are one time, ungraded demonstration items, and while they are recommended for certain events in block, they may be accomplished at any time during the block.

items.title: Brake failure
items.lede: The brake system is a non-boosted, mechanically actuated, hydraulically operated system, independent of the aircraft hydraulic system. The brake system is not affected by a failure of the aircraft hydraulic system.

items.title: Brief and debrief

references.loc: Ch. I §7 — Ground Training and Briefing Requirements
Ch. 2 — Control of Aircraft and Systems

items.lede: The pilot in command should give a preflight briefing for all participating flight crew and ground crew members, if applicable, regarding mission plan and individual responsibilities. The NATOPS list of briefing items is a recommendation of the minimum information a preflight briefing should include, but is not meant to replace local guidelines. After each event, the instructor shall critique the student's performance using cause/effect analysis, particularly with respect to the CTS.

items.title: CDI reverse sensing precautions
items.lede: Normal CDI sensing will be available only if the front course is set into the CDI. The front course is the final approach course depicted for the ILS or LOC approach procedure. On approaches titled LOC BC the depicted FAC is the back course and will result in reverse sensing if set into the CDI.

items.title: CFS and ejection CRM
items.lede: In all cases, once ejection has been called for, if the initiator does not pull the handle in an appropriate amount of time, the other aircrew should initiate. Aircrew do not have a duty to heroically save the aircraft beyond what NATOPS and received training dictates.

items.title: Change of route or destination

events.title: Instrument Navigation
events.label: Change of flight plan while airborne

references.loc: Appendix C §C131 — Requesting Clearance to Alternate
Inside back cover — Change of Flight Plan

items.lede: A helpful format for requesting clearance to an alternate from ATC is the “DRAFT” report. The FAA format for a change of flight plan is printed on the inside back cover of the IFR Supplement.
terms: Change of flight plan while airborne

items.title: Checklist challenge-action response format

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: The checklists will be conducted in the challenge-action-response format. This means you report the **challenge**, accomplish the required **action**, and state the appropriate **response**. As you check each item, place your hand on the item to ensure the desired position is selected.

items.title: Chip detector warning
items.lede: Illumination of the CHIP warning indicates possible metal contamination in the engine oil supply. If the contamination is severe, the engine may fail with little or no further warning.

items.title: Circling maneuver

references.loc: §5.3.5.4 — Criteria for Continuing Instrument Approaches to a Landing
§907 — Airport Surveillance Approach (ASR) and PAR Without Glideslope (PAR W/O GS)

items.lede: The transition to the visual segment on an instrument approach begins once the field is in sight and you are in a safe position to land. Circling only approaches are identified by the navigational system providing final approach guidance and a letter, such as VOR-A, where a straight-in approach is identified by that system and the runway to which the approach is aligned.

items.title: Clearance and departure procedures
items.lede: Once you have filed an IFR flight plan, ATC will approve, disapprove, or revise your plan and provide it to the appropriate controlling agency. An instrument departure is a procedure used to ensure a safe climb out from an airport and to provide safe separation between aircraft. There are four common types of departure.

items.title: Cloud clearances
items.lede: No person may operate an aircraft under VFR when the flight visibility is less, or at a distance from clouds that is less, than that prescribed for the corresponding altitude and class of airspace. Visibility and cloud clearance requirements are different in controlled and uncontrolled airspace.

items.title: Combination maneuvers
items.lede: A Combination Maneuver is nothing more than combining a series of aerobatic maneuvers into a single evolution. A maximum of four maneuvers may be linked together. Perform all maneuvers in accordance with the procedures previously set forth for the maneuvers you intend to fly.

items.title: Constant airspeed climbs and descents
items.lede: Practice maintaining heading and airspeed during climbs and descents. This maneuver will be flown using the same airspeed, power settings and nose attitudes as the Vertical S-1 Pattern. The objective is to stress the concept of using nose attitude to control airspeed during climbs and descents while practicing basic scan and trim skills.

items.title: Contact unusual attitudes

references.loc: §4.4 — Unusual Attitude, Stalls, and Spin Training

items.lede: Recovery may be required due to an improperly flown maneuver, disorientation, area boundaries (lateral or vertical), an aircraft malfunction, or traffic conflicts. In this stage of training you will perform the procedures for recovery from various unusual attitudes utilizing what is primarily a scan of visual references located outside the cockpit. Recovery shall be accomplished by 6000 feet AGL.

items.title: Controlled ejection

references.loc: §3.2 — Actual Emergencies and Precautionary Emergency Landings

items.lede: In controlled (planned) ejection the aircrew controls the time and place of the ejection based on fuel state, weather and other factors. There will be time for both aircrew to run the full controlled ejection checklist, coordinate with a chase aircraft if available, and discuss options with the squadron duty officer, RDO and ATC.

items.title: Crew resource management
items.lede: CRM describes the use of specifically defined behavioral skills as an integral part of every flight to improve mission effectiveness by minimizing crew preventable errors, maximizing crew coordination, and optimizing risk management. It includes all crew members, equipment, and external factors involved in the flight from before the brief to after the debrief. The “Human Error” factor or inadequate CRM is the single leading causal factor for Class A mishaps in modern naval aviation.

items.title: Crosswind computations
items.lede: Accounting for wind when planning takeoff requires that the wind direction and speed be known. The headwind, tailwind, or crosswind component can then be determined using the Takeoff and Landing Crosswind chart in NATOPS Figure A3-6.

items.title: Crosswind full stops
items.lede: During the landing roll, special attention must be given to maintaining directional control with rudders while maintaining crosswind aileron inputs. While the airplane is decelerating during the landing roll, more and more aileron must be applied to keep the upwind wing from rising. When the airplane is coming to a stop, the aileron control must be held fully towards the winds.

items.title: Crosswind limits

references.loc: Ch. A3 — Takeoff and Landing Crosswind

items.lede: The maximum demonstrated dry runway crosswind for takeoff and landing is 25 knots. The maximum permissible crosswind is 10 knots for a wet runway, and 5 knots for an icy runway. Maximum tailwind component for takeoff is 10 knots.

items.title: Crosswind takeoff and landings
items.lede: The procedures for a takeoff with a crosswind are the same as for a no wind takeoff, except aileron is held into the wind to keep the wings level. Throughout the final, flare and touchdown, the aircraft should track in a straight line down the runway. The application of crosswind correction must be continued as necessary during the landing transition and flare to prevent drift.

items.title: Crosswind touch-and-goes
items.lede: Hold crosswind inputs on the deck and apply upwind aileron to maintain a wings level attitude. Initiate positive, firm, rotation when flying speed is reached to avoid side-slipping.

items.title: Cruise maneuvering
items.lede: Cruise maneuvering will build on the two dimensional fundamentals learned while adding the challenge of maneuvering in the vertical plane as well. During VMC parade turns into and away, Wing was limited to one side or the other from Lead while conducting level turns. Cruise maneuvering will use a fixed power setting, but Wing will now have the ability to change sides as required, using radius of turn principles to maintain the 60° cruise bearing line.

items.title: Day emergency procedures
items.lede: Although emergency procedures must be handled in accordance with NATOPS Flight Manual procedures, special provisions may exist for Visual Navigation sorties. All Navigation routes include a Minimum Safe Altitude for each leg of the planned route and an Emergency Route Abort Altitude for the entire route of flight. A cool head is the pilot's best asset should they become temporarily disoriented. Some situations may dictate an unplanned stop at one of the emergency fields marked on the chart.

items.title: DD-175-1 weather brief
items.lede: DD-175-1 flight route weather briefings will include briefing (flimsy) number and brief void time. DD-175-1 briefs are only valid up to 3.0 hours past briefing/FWB delivery time or ETD plus one-half hour.

items.title: DD-1801

references.loc: §4-5 — DD Form 1801-C, DoD International Flight Plan (Continuation)

items.lede: The DD-1801 (DoD International Flight Plan), completed in accordance with FLIP General Planning, may be used for other than local flights originating from airfields in the United States at which a military operations department is located. A completed flight plan will be submitted to flight planning personnel, either in-person or electronically, for entry into the ARTCC system.

items.title: Destination maintenance facilities and operating procedures

events.title: Day Navigation
events.label: Destination maintenance facilities and operating procedures

references.loc: Ch. 1 §7 — Cross Country and Special Procedures
Appendix A — TW-4 CDO/ODO Aircraft Off-Station Checklist
Appendix B — Squadron CDO/ODO Aircraft Off-Station Checklist
Appendix E — T-6B Dropped Ejection Seat Safety Pin Procedures

items.lede: An off-station aircraft is any aircraft that does not return to KNGP as intended. When an aircraft has a problem off station, the AC notifies their squadron's Command Duty Officer, who in turn notifies the TW-4 CDO. The Wing CDO finalizes the recovery plan with CNATRA DET, who coordinates with the contracted maintenance department.
terms: Destination maintenance facilities and operating procedures

items.title: Direct to a VOR

references.loc: §600 — Direct to a VOR or FMS Waypoint

items.lede: The process used to proceed from your current position direct to a VOR or FMS waypoint. Both versions place the head of the bearing pointer under the heading index on the HSI, then track the new course flying a heading that keeps the CDI centered.

items.title: Discontinued entry
items.lede: Two-way radio communication with the RDO or crash crew is required for entry into the traffic pattern at an outlying field. A discontinued entry must be executed immediately if the RDO directs one, if the RDO has not acknowledged the aircraft's initial call by 2 NM from the runway threshold, if the aircraft is lined up on the wrong runway, if a PPEL/P is not in sight by 2 NM from the runway threshold or is a conflict, or if the aircraft is past the upwind numbers and interval is in doubt. Aircraft executing a discontinued entry outside of 2 NM must immediately turn away from the normal traffic pattern a minimum of 90 degrees off the inbound runway heading.

items.title: Divert to alternate

references.loc: Inside back cover — Change of Flight Plan

items.lede: A divert to the filed alternate is one of the options after a missed approach. The DRAFT mnemonic is useful in formatting the request for clearance to an alternate from ATC. Changing the flight plan through a Flight Service Station instead takes the format printed on the inside back cover of the IFR Supplement.

items.title: DOR/TTO policy
items.lede: CNATRAINST 1500.4 (series) defines the conditions under which a Training Time Out (TTO) may be requested. A TTO may be called in any training situation whenever a student or instructor expresses concern for personal safety or a need for clarification of procedures or requirements exists. Training Time-Out/Drop on Request policy is in effect, and students are briefed on drop on request, training time out and high risk training safety policies during the Naval Aviation Survival Training Program overview.

items.title: Dual concurrence/response CRM

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: Not every step requires a dual response; however, each pilot, regardless of the seat that they occupy, must ensure each step of the checklist has been accomplished. Items shown as (BOTH) within the checklist indicate dual concurrence is required.

items.title: Ejection seat and CFS

numbers.label: Seat capability
numbers.value: zero-zero to 35,000 feet, up to approximately 370 KIAS

references.loc: Ch. 1 — Shoulder Harness Reel and Control
Ch. 1 — Sea Water Activated Release System (SEAWARS)

items.lede: The aircraft is equipped with Martin-Baker ejection seats. Each ejection seat is fully automatic, providing safe escape for most combinations of aircraft altitude, speed, attitude, and flight path within the aircraft operational envelope. The seat is capable of providing safe escape from zero altitude, zero speed, up to 35,000 feet at speeds up to approximately 370 KIAS. An interseat sequencing system (ISS) selector is located in the aft cockpit which permits the selection of solo or dual ejection modes. The aircraft uses a dual redundant canopy fracturing system (CFS) to provide a clear path for the pilot(s) during ejection or emergency ground egress.

items.title: Ejection

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Use of Terrain Clearance Charts

items.lede: Within the design specification, with correct body posture, ejection is a very safe means of egress. There are three ways to think of ejection: immediate, time critical, and controlled (planned). Understanding which of these three scenarios the aircrew is in based on time is essential to making the best decision. If the aircraft is not controllable, ejection must be accomplished regardless of speed, altitude, or attitude since immediate ejection offers the best opportunity for survival.

items.title: Electrical system malfunctions

numbers.label: GEN RESET switch, depress and hold
Starter left ON in MANUAL drains battery in
Main battery with generator bus shed

items.lede: The BUS TIE switch is used to tie/isolate the battery and generator buses. With the BUS TIE switch engaged (NORM position), the generator feeds both generator and battery bus items. If the bus tie fails, or is set to OPEN, the amber BUS TIE caution on the EICAS illuminates, separating the battery and generator buses. If the battery or battery bus fails (red BAT BUS warning on the EICAS illuminated) while the BUS TIE caution is illuminated, items on the battery bus will not be powered. In an emergency situation, the auxiliary battery powers the backup flight instrument, radio relays, Inertial Reference Unit (IRU), standby VHF control, and FIRE 1 fire warning system for approximately 30 minutes.

items.title: Electrical system

numbers.label: Battery bus power, BUS TIE open

items.lede: The electrical system includes a 28 VDC, 300 amp starter/generator, an aerobatic 24 VDC lead-acid battery, a 24 VDC auxiliary battery, and an external power receptacle. Electrical power is distributed through the battery and generator buses connected by the bus tie switch.

items.title: Emergency engine shutdown on the ground

events.title: Familiarization Cockpit Procedures
events.label: Emergency engine shutdown on the ground

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground

items.lede: In the event of an engine fire, prop strike, or chip light; if the aircraft appears likely to depart the prepared surface; or should any other serious ground emergency occur, accomplish the Emergency Engine Shutdown On The Ground procedure.
terms: Emergency engine shutdown on the ground

items.title: Emergency field selection
items.lede: The first reaction to any emergency encountered in the low level environment is "climb to cope". If the engine fails on a low level, recovery is unlikely unless a suitable landing field is within approximately 3 miles. Chart study for potential emergency diverts before the mission will greatly enhance chances for success.

items.title: Emergency ground egress
items.lede: If emergency egress is required on the ground, perform the Emergency Ground Egress procedure after the aircraft has come to a complete stop and the engine has been shut down.

items.title: Emergency landing pattern
items.lede: The ELP is a 360° pattern designed to position the aircraft for landing at a prepared surface during a complete power loss (Forced Landing) or when an impending engine failure exists in which sufficient power for continued flight is available (Precautionary Emergency Landing [PEL]). The ELP is used for both actual/simulated PEL and actual/simulated Forced Landings. If altitude permits, intercept the ELP at 3000 feet AGL (2500 feet AGL minimum per the T-6B Flight Manual). High key and low key are positions over the ground, not altitudes.

items.title: Emergency orbit pattern

numbers.label: Remain at or above Delta until

items.lede: The Delta Pattern is a racetrack pattern that is oriented around the duty runway and flown in the same direction as the normal landing pattern. Aircraft are required to enter the Delta Pattern by direction of the RDO during runway changes or as required during emergencies. Delta altitude at Goliad is 2300 ft MSL; at NAS Corpus Christi the Delta pattern is flown at 2000 ft MSL and conforms to the pattern for the runway in use.

items.title: En route descent
items.lede: In the enroute structure, the FAA expects the pilot to descend at an optimum rate consistent with the operating characteristics of the aircraft to 1000 feet above the assigned altitude, and then attempt to descend at a rate of 500 to 1500 FPM until the assigned altitude is reached.

items.title: En route fuel management

references.loc: Ch. 1 — Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System (EICAS)

items.lede: During flight, compare estimated values for times, groundspeed, fuel flow, etc., with the actual values observed. Check fuel quantity/balance at initial level-off and periodically during the flight. When fuel endurance is a factor, refer to the Maximum Endurance data in NATOPS Appendix A.

items.title: En route procedures
items.lede: Due to the increasing complexity of the air traffic system, the terminal phase can be one of the more challenging phases of flight. To maintain constant situational awareness and avoid task saturation, the pilot must know the procedures and stay ahead of the aircraft. To aid in task management, as you approach and enter your terminal area, the mnemonic ABCD can be useful.

items.title: En route weather sources
items.lede: Pilots shall periodically determine that their intended route of flight remains clear of aviation Severe Weather Watch Bulletins and that weather forecasts for each successive intermediate destination and alternate, when required, continue to satisfy the minimums established for the aircraft and the filing status.

items.title: Energy management

numbers.label: Level deceleration, per 10 knots above 125 KIAS

items.lede: Energy management is planning a sortie profile that allows maneuvers to be accomplished in an order that optimizes time and energy. Energy level is defined by airspeed (kinetic energy) and altitude (potential energy) and is manipulated with power, drag, and G-loading. Plan maneuvers in an order that minimize the requirement for deliberate energy changes, and make use of the inherent energy gaining or losing properties of individual maneuvers.

items.title: Engine air starts

numbers.label: Airstart envelope, sea level to 15,000 feet
Altitude lost per attempt at 125 KIAS
Discontinue if no N1 rise within
Abort if no ITT rise within

items.lede: Three airstart procedures are approved for this aircraft: PMU NORM; PMU OFF; and Immediate Airstart (PMU NORM). The status of the PMU dictates the type of airstart attempted. All airstarts are starter assisted. If the airstart is successful, useful power will be available after 40 seconds from starter engagement.

items.title: Engine failure during flight

numbers.label: Level deceleration, per 10 knots above 125 KIAS
Do not delay ejection decision below
Oil pressure, engine seized or not

items.lede: In the event of an engine failure, a decision to eject, land, or airstart must be made. The altitude at which the engine fails will determine the time available to perform the procedures.

items.title: Engine failure immediately after takeoff

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Engine Failure Immediately After Takeoff (Sufficient Runway Remaining Straight Ahead)

items.lede: A complete engine failure immediately after takeoff is an extremely critical emergency requiring immediate action and decision making by the pilot. In all cases, control the aircraft energy state through prudent use of altitude, airspeed, and configuration.

items.title: Engine failure indications

numbers.label: N1 does not indicate speeds below

items.lede: Initial indications of engine failure or flameout are loss of power and airspeed, rapid decay in N1, torque and ITT, and propeller movement towards feather. The GEN, FUEL PX, and OIL PX warning will illuminate, followed by the OBOGS FAIL warning. Gear and flaps will remain in the last selected position at the time of engine failure.

items.title: Engine malfunctions

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Engine Failure Immediately After Takeoff (Sufficient Runway Remaining Straight Ahead)
Ch. 3 — Uncommanded Power Changes/Loss of Power/Uncommanded Propeller Feather

items.lede: In the event of an engine failure, a decision to eject, land, or airstart must be made. Illumination of the FIRE annunciator indicates the possibility of fire in the engine compartment.

items.title: Engine system
items.lede: The PT6A-68 is a free-turbine turboprop engine flat rated to produce 1100 shaft horsepower (SHP) as installed in the aircraft. The engine is a reverse-flow design with two independent sections: the gas generator section and the power turbine section. The gas generator section (the aft half of the engine) consists of the four-stage axial-flow compressor, single-stage centrifugal flow compressor, combustion chamber, and single-stage compressor turbine. The power section (the forward half of the engine) consists of the two-stage axial-flow power turbine, exhaust case, and reduction gearbox.

items.title: FAF-to-MAP timing adjustments
items.lede: The aerodrome sketch is provided on each approach plate in either the lower left-hand or right-hand corner. The timing “FAF to MAP” information at the bottom of the sketch is used to determine the timing from the FAF to the MAP, at various ground speeds. Where the groundspeed is not one of the tabulated values, the timing must be interpolated.

items.title: Fan break
items.lede: There are two methods of executing the break: interval break or fan break. The fan break is an alternate entry method, initiated with interval by Lead giving the "follow me" signal to Wing.

items.title: Feeder fixes
items.lede: Feeder fixes put the aircraft on an intercept heading and altitude to be maintained until established on the localizer course. They are one of the transition procedures that establish the aircraft onto the final approach course.

items.title: Feeder routes
items.lede: A feeder route provides a direct course from the enroute fix or NAVAID to the appropriate IF or IAF. At least one is provided from an airway fix or NAVAID to the TAA boundary where a portion of the TAA does not underlie an airway.

items.title: Feet to rudder placement
items.lede: When using the rudder pedals, pressure should be applied smoothly and evenly by pressing with the ball of one foot just as when using the brakes of an automobile. The feet come off the brakes for the takeoff roll and for touchdown.

items.title: Fire on ground
items.lede: The primary indications of an engine fire are illumination of the FIRE annunciators. When evidence of a fire exists during start or other ground operations, perform the Emergency Engine Shutdown On The Ground procedure and Emergency Ground Egress procedure if applicable.

items.title: Fire warning in flight
items.lede: Illumination of the FIRE annunciator indicates the possibility of fire in the engine compartment. Pending confirmation of an engine fire, initiate PEL procedures with the intention of landing as soon as possible.

items.title: Flap failures

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Controllability Check (Structural Damage/Flight Control Malfunction)

items.lede: If uncommanded lateral rolling or yawing is experienced during operation of the wing flaps, an asymmetric (split-flap) condition likely exists. Flap asymmetry may occur from physical binding of one or more of the four flap segments or from a failure of the torque link between the inner and outer flap segments. Sufficient control authority exists to counteract yaw and roll at pattern airspeeds.

items.title: Flight gear check

references.loc: Ch. IV — FAM21, Familiarization Cockpit Procedures
Ch. IV — FAM22, Familiarization Emergency Procedures Trainer

items.lede: With survival vest on, the student shall locate, identify, and discuss function of each ALSS item.

items.title: Flight Service Station

references.loc: Appendix C §C102 — Initial Contact or Callup
Section B §1 — FAA Air Traffic Control Procedures
Section C §8 — FAA Pilot-to-Weather Briefer Service

items.lede: Flight Service Specialists are qualified and certified by the NWS as Pilot Weather Briefers. At non-military fields, you may have to file your flight plan with a Flight Service Station (FSS). NOTAM information can be obtained from the FSS.

items.title: Flight split
items.lede: The objective of an in-flight split is to split up a formation so that individual aircraft can safely separate into different working blocks to facilitate single ship high work training. Safe separation can be attained through the use of visual, altitude, lateral, heading, airspeed, or timing differentials. Most commonly, it is best to use a combination of Altitude and Heading separation to achieve a safe flight split.

items.title: FMS arrivals

references.loc: Ch. 1 — Standard Terminal Arrival Route (STAR) Selection

items.lede: The complete arrival procedure, including standard arrival route and STAR transition, can be loaded into the route at the same time or in segments, depending on the ATC clearance received. The segments are selected from lists of named procedures extracted from the navigation database for the destination airport. On entering the terminal area the FMS transitions to the terminal phase of flight, and approach transitions are appended to the route after the STAR.

items.title: FMS flight plan usage

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: FMS flight plan usage (SID/STAR, holding, and approach)

items.lede: Stored routes and manually created routes require an origin and destination airport, but do not contain a departure or arrival procedure. Standard Instrument Departures, Standard Terminal Arrivals and approaches are added to a route from the DEP/ARR page. Pilots are not authorized to fly a published RNAV (GPS) instrument approach procedure, departure procedure, or arrival procedure unless it is retrievable by the procedure name from a current aircraft navigation database and conforms to the charted procedure.
terms: FMS flight plan usage (SID/STAR, holding, and approach)

items.title: FMS procedures
items.lede: The flight management system provides extensive functionality for navigation, flight planning, communications, navigation radio tuning, and simple route and flight plan creation and modification procedures. This functionality is provided using the MFD and UFCP controls.

items.title: Forced landing
items.lede: Forced Landing procedures should be executed while intercepting or maintaining the ELP profile to recover the aircraft when the engine is not available, and an airstart is not attempted or unsuccessful. The Forced Landing is flown with the engine inoperative (no power), or when power is insufficient for continued flight.

items.title: Formation arrival and departure procedures
items.lede: Once safely airborne, Lead levels off to clear the pattern complying with local course rules departure procedures; once clear of the pattern, Lead sets 80% torque and climbs at 160 KIAS until Wing is in position. The recovery will generally be a VMC recovery via local course rules for the break entry. Approaching the initial VFR entry point, Lead will direct Wing to the Parade Position with enough time to get stabilized prior to the break, then give Wing the appropriate visual signal and conduct the break with clearance from tower.

items.title: Formation communications
items.lede: Your visual or radio communications within the flight must be clear and timely to avoid confusion. The flight will essentially use two call signs: an ATC call sign to communicate with outside agencies and a tactical (TAC) call sign selected by the flight for inter-flight communications. The Formation Lead will conduct all communications with outside controlling agencies, and Wing will monitor and back Lead up as necessary. Lead and Wing must always have direct communication with each other via the pre-briefed tactical frequency, which is confirmed with a positive check-in each time the tactical frequency is changed.

items.title: Formation emergency procedures
items.lede: There are additional considerations when handling emergency situations in formation. As Lead, remember to take into account all actions that will affect the Wing. As Wingman, maintain situational awareness at all times and be ready to assist as requested. In formation, the greatest immediate threat during an emergency is a mid-air collision within the flight. The threat can be alleviated by immediately communicating and taking additional separation, weather permitting, as appropriate.

items.title: Formation maneuvers
items.lede: Parade Position is the basis for all maneuvers in this chapter. It is a fixed position on the left or right 45° bearing from Lead with sufficient wingtip clearance and step-down, utilizing the checkpoints below. Once the flight is established in the area and Ops Checks are complete, the parade sequence begins: a series of tasks which allow both students the opportunity to practice flying basic formation positions and maneuvers.

items.title: Formation position corrections
items.lede: Good formation flying is the result of anticipation and the use of small, timely corrections about all three axes. Strive to maintain perfect positioning, but understand that Wing will only be there for a fleeting moment. What makes a good formation pilot is the ability to recognize and limit deviations and make timely and efficient corrections.

items.title: Formation preflight planning
items.lede: Teamwork is an essential element to good formation. Studying, setting up a briefing space, briefing, pre-flight, post-flight, and debrief should all be a team effort, and these ground procedures are common to all formation flights. Aircraft issue and preflight will be conducted in the same manner as any syllabus flight. Knowing the fuel state of both aircraft at all times is essential.

items.title: Formation squadron SOP

numbers.label: VMC if circling is not authorized

references.loc: Ch. 1 §9 — Bird Aircraft Strike Hazard (BASH) Program

items.lede: Formation flights must not enter Instrument Meteorological Conditions from VFR on top unless the reported weather at the destination airport meets circling approach minimums for the runway in use, and at least one T-6B formation qualified IP should be airborne on a local VFR event when solos are airborne. Both squadrons prohibit formation flights at night, and each sets its own requirement for flying formation in IMC: VT-27 requires an IP at the controls, VT-28 requires FORM/X qualification to fly as wing.

items.title: Fuel cutoff gate finger lift guard

events.title: Familiarization Flight 0
events.label: Fuel cutoff gate finger lift guard

items.lede: The PCL incorporates a cutoff gate to prevent inadvertent engine shutdown. In aircraft after the power quadrant assembly modification, the finger lift guard is pushed down before the PCL cutoff finger lift is raised.
terms: Fuel cutoff gate finger lift guard

items.title: Fuel planning
items.lede: Knowing the fuel state of both aircraft at all times is essential. Lead must know the aircraft with the lowest fuel state in the flight for planning purposes, and the same information is critical if Wing has to assume the Lead. To determine the flight's fuel state, Lead will direct Operations Checks, commonly referred to as "Ops Checks", at various points during the flight, then use the lowest fuel state in the flight for planning purposes. Understanding the definitions of Joker, Bingo, and Divert Fuel is required.

items.title: Fuel system

numbers.label: Additional if filled over the wing
Auto balance activates
numbers.value: 20 pounds or more for more than 30 seconds

items.lede: The fuel system provides approximately 1100 pounds of usable fuel through the single-point refueling system. Three integral tanks built into a single-piece wing provide fuel storage. The fuel system incorporates an auto balance system to keep the fuel level in the wing tanks within 20 pounds of each other.

items.title: Full-stop landings
items.lede: Land smoothly on the main-mounts at the Intended Point of Landing on runway centerline. Landing is divided into three phases: landing transition, flare and touchdown, and landing roll. Each of these phases serves as a transition from the previous phase to the next. The landing roll serves as the transition from landing to taxi, and airspeed is reduced straight-ahead on the runway until at safe taxi speed.

items.title: GCA pattern
items.lede: In addition to developing basic airwork scan and trim skills, the GCA maneuver incorporates many of the basic skill sets required during execution of a Radar Ground Controlled Approach. In the descent, remember, nose controls airspeed, power controls rate of descent.

items.title: Gear emergencies

numbers.label: Do not slow below
numbers.value: 90 KIAS or stick shaker, whichever is higher

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Landing with Unsafe Gear Indications
Ch. 3 — Landing with Cocked Nose Wheel
§6.3.2 — Procedure for Checking Wheels Down and Locked

items.lede: Execute the Landing Gear Malfunction checklist anytime the landing gear does not indicate fully up with the gear handle up, or fully down with the gear handle down. If any safe gear-down indications are obtained at any point, discontinue the checklist and land as soon as practical.

items.title: GPS allowable operations

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: GPS allowable operations (GPS waypoints in lieu of NDB, VOR, and TACAN fixes)

items.lede: An FAA approved FMS or GPS system may be used to navigate to, identify, or hold at any waypoints retrieved from an FAA approved and current database. It cannot be used to navigate the final segment, lateral navigation, of any approach that does not have GPS in the title.
terms: GPS allowable operations (GPS waypoints in lieu of NDB, VOR, and TACAN fixes)

items.title: GPS approaches
items.lede: All approaches that contain GPS in the title can be flown using GPS. GPS-equipped aircraft do not need underlying ground-based NAVAIDs or associated aircraft avionics to fly the approach, and monitoring the underlying approach with ground-based NAVAIDs is suggested when able.

items.title: GPS flight modes

numbers.label: En route scale

numbers.label: Terminal at
