items.lede: On entering the terminal area, the FMS transitions to the terminal phase of flight. On leaving the terminal area, the FMS changes from terminal to en-route phase of flight. When a valid GPS approach has been selected and loaded into the active flight plan from the navigation database, the approach phase of flight is activated automatically 2 nm prior to the final approach fix.

items.title: GPS holding
items.lede: An FAA approved FMS or GPS system may be used to navigate to, identify, or hold at any waypoints retrieved from an FAA approved and current database. Holding can be accomplished at an intersection, GPS waypoint, Radial/DME fix, or at a navigation facility. The abeam position is a position directly abeam the holding fix on the outbound leg. A bold standard racetrack holding pattern (HILO) may be provided at the IAF.

items.title: GPS procedures
items.lede: Area navigation is a method of navigation which permits aircraft operation on any desired flight path within the coverage of ground-based or space-based navigation aids. Pilots are not authorized to fly a published RNAV (GPS) instrument approach procedure, departure procedure, or arrival procedure unless it is retrievable by the procedure name from a current aircraft navigation database and conforms to the charted procedure.

items.title: ATF, ATS, CTS and MIF
items.lede: The standards outlined in Chapter IX, Course Training Standards, are used to evaluate student performance of individual items and maneuvers. MIFs identify the minimum acceptable level of performance in relation to the CTS that must be achieved at the completion of each training block. Instructor pilots shall evaluate student performance against these standards.

items.title: Ground handling signals

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: Communications will be conducted visually whenever practical, provided no sacrifice in operational efficiency is involved. Ground handling signals are shown in NATOPS Figure 8-4-1.

items.title: Ground-speed calculations

references.loc: Appendix B — 60-to-1 Rule and Other Formulas

items.lede: At 60 NM from a NAVAID the distance between each radial is approximately 1 NM.

items.title: Half cuban eight
items.lede: This maneuver is a combination of a slightly modified Loop and Immelmann. The maneuver is complete at level flight, with entry airspeed and on reciprocal heading. Select a long, well defined section line which extends behind as well as in front of you.

items.title: Hand signals
items.lede: Your visual or radio communications within the flight must be clear and timely to avoid confusion. The Wingman should have time to acknowledge the signal before Lead executes the maneuver.

items.title: Hard landings
items.lede: Exceeding NATOPS limits for rate of descent at touchdown can lead to structural damage and landing gear component failure. In case of a hard landing, do not raise the gear.

items.title: Headwork
items.lede: Headwork and situational awareness is one of the Universally Graded Items, graded on all complete syllabus events. The behavior statement is to maintain situational awareness, and the standard is to demonstrate the ability to minimize the effects of adverse factors and capitalize on opportunities to avoid mission degradation.

items.title: Heavy-weight landing considerations
items.lede: At higher aircraft weights, higher airspeed may be required to prevent slowing below on-speed (amber donut) AOA indication. Above 700-800 pounds of fuel, approximately 3-5 knots above the 120/115/110 approach turn airspeeds may be required. Heavy aircraft are less responsive to pitch and power changes, and develop sink rates quicker than light aircraft.

items.title: HEFOE
items.lede: HEFOE is a method of signaling system failure when NORDO, using hand signals during the day or a flashlight at night. In the event aircrew encounter an in-flight emergency while NORDO, they will pass the condition of the aircraft to the other aircraft using HEFOE hand signals. The use of HEFOE signals assumes that one or both aircraft are NORDO.

items.title: High altitude approach
items.lede: A high altitude instrument approach enables an aircraft to transition from the high altitude structure to the final approach course for landing. These approaches are routinely executed by high performance military aircraft into military aerodromes to maintain efficient fuel consumption, higher TAS, and to avoid low altitude weather until closer to the destination.

items.title: HILO approach
items.lede: The Holding Pattern Approach, or Holding In Lieu Of procedure turn, is a type of procedure turn. The HILO approach uses a published holding pattern to reverse course and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course. HILO approaches are printed using a normal holding pattern track with a heavy line indicating in lieu of procedure turn. Unlike the teardrop and procedure turn approaches, the holding pattern approach will always have a FAF depicted on the approach.

items.title: Holding corrections
items.lede: Compensate for wind effects by flying drift corrected headings on the inbound and outbound legs while making appropriate timing adjustments. Adjust outbound heading and time to compensate for wind so that the turn inbound will place the aircraft on the holding course and, where leg lengths are established by timing, with an appropriate amount of inbound time.

items.title: Holding entry
items.lede: Upon arrival at the holding fix, the entry turn will be made towards the general direction given in the holding clearance. The specific heading needed to establish the aircraft in the designated holding airspace is determined by the type of holding pattern being used, standard pattern or non-standard pattern, and by comparing aircraft heading with the reciprocal of the holding course. There are three basic types of entry turns: parallel, teardrop and direct.

items.title: Holding

numbers.label: Inbound leg at or below 14,000 feet

items.lede: Holding is a predetermined maneuver that keeps aircraft within a specified airspace until further clearance is received from ATC. It can be accomplished at an intersection, GPS waypoint, radial/DME fix, or at a navigation facility. When ATC clears you to hold, a specified airspace oriented around the holding fix has been reserved, clear of other traffic. The extent of the cleared airspace is based on maximum holding airspeed as listed in the FLIP GP and FAA AIM.

items.title: Home field arrival
items.lede: Unless otherwise noted, fly all arrival procedures at 240 KIAS until reaching Point SHAMROCK. At PT SHAMROCK, slow to 200 KIAS, contact Navy Corpus Tower (CH 4 UHF) and state intentions. Turn towards and report the runway numbers for the Overhead Maneuver or final for the Straight-in approach.

items.title: Hot start

numbers.label: Abort if ITT likely to exceed
Abort if ITT likely to remain

items.lede: In the AUTO start mode, if a hot start is projected, the PMU should terminate the start sequence. The engine start should be aborted manually if ITT rate of increase appears likely to exceed 1000 °C, or if ITT appears likely to remain between 871-1000 °C for > 5 seconds.

items.title: HSI orientation
items.lede: For overall orientation, consider the VOR station always located at the center of the HSI card and the aircraft's position on the tail of the bearing pointer. The VOR provides 360 magnetic courses called radials, which radiate from the station like spokes from the hub of a wheel. Unless the bearing pointer is on the heading index, as the aircraft moves forward, heads will fall and tails will rise.

items.title: HUD
items.lede: The HUD in the forward cockpit and the HUD repeater on the right MFD provide display of aircraft flight, navigation and tactical data; simulated weapon inventory and status indication; ARM/SAFE/SIM condition; a fixed steering cue for manual weapon employment; and air-to-air and air-to-ground weapon employment solutions and steering commands.

items.title: Hung start

numbers.label: Auto-abort if N1 acceleration to idle

items.lede: In the AUTO start mode, if a hung start is projected, the PMU should terminate the start sequence. The engine start should be aborted manually if normal N1 increase is halted.

items.title: Hydraulic system malfunctions
items.lede: Normal operation of landing gear, flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering should be considered unavailable when the HYD FL LO caution is illuminated and pressure is below 1800 psi, or when hydraulic pressure is rapidly decreasing toward or reads 0 psi. When the EHYD PX LO caution is illuminated, the emergency landing gear and flap extension system should be considered inoperative.

items.title: Hydraulic system
items.lede: The hydraulic system consists of one engine-driven pump with approximately a 5 quart capacity. The hydraulic pump pressurizes the normal system and emergency accumulator to 3000±120 psi through a hydraulic fuse and one-way check valve. Once pressure exceeds 1800 psi, the system can power the landing gear, main gear doors, flaps, speed brake, and nose wheel steering. Emergency hydraulic pressure is available after the normal system has pressurized the emergency accumulator. Pulling the emergency gear extension handle releases the emergency accumulator pressure through independent emergency lines to extend the landing gear and flaps.

items.title: Hyperventilation and hypoxia
items.lede: Hypoxia is a general term that describes a state of oxygen deficiency in the tissues. Hypocapnia is low CO2 in the blood resulting from hyperventilation. Adverse physiological conditions have common symptoms similar to other adverse physiological conditions, making it difficult to discern the root cause of physiological symptoms during flight.

items.title: IAC failure
items.lede: The dual IACs (IAC 1 and IAC 2) form the core of the integrated avionics system, integrating the various components of the system as well as providing backup capability. The information from the IACs is presented by three MFDs in each cockpit. IAC data crosstalk malfunction can result in a loss of synchronization between cockpits.

items.title: Icing
items.lede: The aircraft has been approved only for transit through light rime icing conditions. Prolonged flight in known icing conditions is prohibited and must be avoided. The aircraft includes protection for critical systems and cockpit displays through the use of heated pitot masts and a heated angle-of-attack sensor.

items.title: IFR clearance from uncontrolled airports

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: Obtaining IFR clearance from uncontrolled airports

references.loc: §5-2-7 — Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times

items.lede: Where there is no clearance delivery, an IFR clearance may be obtained in one of several ways, and which are available is listed for the field in the IFR Supplement. A clearance obtained on the ground may carry a void time, and you must be airborne before it.
terms: Obtaining IFR clearance from uncontrolled airports

items.title: IFR flight planning

events.title: Instrument Check Flight
events.label: Flight planning (submit a completed DD-1801 and jet log: Stopover flight plan to include an en route holding delay (1st leg), and terminal delay (2nd leg))

references.loc: §4.5.5 — Stopover Flights Within the Contiguous United States
Ch. V — I44, Instrument Check Flight
Ch. 4 §7 — SNA Navigation Mission Planning Requirements

items.lede: Before commencing a flight, the pilot in command shall be familiar with all available information appropriate to the intended operation. It is important to not focus solely on the FTI, but incorporate information from all available sources, both military and civilian: CNAF 3710, the FAR/AIM, the FIH, General Planning, Area Planning, NATOPS servicing, local SOPs, Wing Stan Notes and cross-country instructions.
terms: Flight planning (submit a completed DD-1801 and jet log: Stopover flight plan to include an en route holding delay (1st leg), and terminal delay (2nd leg))

items.title: IFR pick-up
items.lede: Departing VFR and picking the IFR clearance up in the air. Until a change of flight plan is filed and an IFR clearance obtained, the flight remains in VFR conditions.

items.title: IFR Supplement
items.lede: The IFR Supplement is the DOD Airport Directory, one of the Flight Information Publications carried for an instrument flight. After the general information it is divided into three major sections: the Airport/Facility Directory Legend, the Airport/Facility Directory, and Theater Flight Data and Procedures. The inside back cover has the FAA formats for position reports, change of flight plan, and filing flight plans in flight.

items.title: IFR to VFR transition

references.loc: Appendix D — CTW-4 Closed Tower Operating Procedures

items.lede: It is the responsibility of the pilot in command to ensure that the proper agency is notified of flight termination. Cancellation of an instrument flight plan does not meet the requirement for closing out the flight plan; when a landing report has been properly delivered, the flight plan will be considered closed out.

items.title: IFR unusual attitudes
items.lede: Recognize and recover from an unusual attitude with reference to instruments only. An unusual attitude is any unexpected or inadvertent attitude encountered during normal instrument flight. Use the attitude indicator as the main recovery instrument after its proper operation is verified and an unusual attitude is confirmed. The recovery is complete when the desired attitude for normal instrument flight is attained.

items.title: ILS approach
items.lede: The Instrument Landing System is a precision approach system that provides azimuth and glideslope information to the pilot. It consists of a highly directional localizer and glideslope transmitter with associated marker beacons, compass locators, and at some sites, Distance Measuring Equipment. The system is automatically monitored and provides changeover to a standby localizer or glideslope transmitter when the main system malfunctions. Because both course and glidepath information is provided, it constitutes a precision approach and DA/DH minimums may be used.

items.title: ILS full procedure turn
items.lede: Because of the highly localized broadcast area, the ILS course and glidepath signals cannot be displayed until on or very near to the final approach course. As such they require transition procedures to establish the aircraft onto final, and the procedure turn approach is one of them. Normal CDI sensing will be available only if the front course is set into the CDI.

items.title: IMC emergencies

references.loc: Section A §1 — Recommended Procedures for Any Emergency Phase
Ch. 3 — Smoke and Fume Elimination/Electrical Fire

items.lede: The flight manual provides the best possible operating instructions under most circumstances, but it is not a substitute for sound judgement. Multiple emergencies, adverse weather, terrain, etc. may require modification of the procedures.

items.title: Immediate air-start

numbers.label: Airstart envelope
numbers.value: 125 to 200 KIAS, sea level to 15,000 feet

numbers.label: Discontinue if no N1 rise in
Abort if no ITT rise in

items.lede: Three airstart procedures are approved for this aircraft: PMU NORM; PMU OFF; and Immediate Airstart (PMU NORM). The Immediate Airstart (PMU NORM) procedure should be used following engine failure at low altitude when thrust requirements are critical, or when time and conditions do not permit completing a full airstart procedure.

items.title: Immelmann
items.lede: The Immelmann is a half Loop followed by a half roll, all flown in the same vertical plane. The maneuver is complete after a momentary pause in level flight with wings level on an opposite heading from entry. This maneuver offers a quick means of reversing the direction of flight while trading excess airspeed for increased altitude.

items.title: Impending engine failure indications
items.lede: Indications of an impending engine failure could be excessive vibration, smoke or fumes, chip detector annunciator light, fuel or propeller malfunction, or any other condition listed in the NATOPS requiring that you land as soon as possible via PEL. The PEL procedure should be executed whenever indications of a possible engine failure exist.

items.title: I'M SAFE checklist

references.loc: §8.3.2.1.1 — Crew Rest for Flight Crew and Flight Support Personnel

items.lede: "I'M SAFE" is a simple checklist to determine if we are ready and fit to fly. As a rule, proper aircrew coordination begins with the individual crew member, and our situational awareness might be diminished even before we set foot in the cockpit.

items.title: Inadvertent instrument flight
items.lede: If a formation flight inadvertently enters IMC conditions, Lead will transition to an instrument scan. If unable to return to VMC, ensure proper terrain clearance and contact ATC to pick up an IFR clearance for the flight, or separate clearances for each individual aircraft.

items.title: Inadvertent thunderstorm penetration
items.lede: Flights through thunderstorms or other areas of extreme turbulence should be avoided due to the possibility of engine flameout, structural failure, or damage due to hail, lightning, and violent up and down drafts. Should flight through an area of thunderstorm activity become unavoidable, the following procedures should be used.

items.title: Inadvertent trim actuation
items.lede: Secondary flight controls include electrically actuated pitch/roll/yaw trim systems and a rudder trim aid device (TAD). The Trim Interrupt button on the control stick will remove electrical power from the trim devices and is used during certain trim malfunctions.

items.title: Incipient spin recovery
items.lede: Incipient spins are the spin-like motion that occurs between a post-stall gyration and a fully developed spin. The incipient spin phase lasts approximately two turns. In order to recover from the incipient spin, execute the INADVERTENT DEPARTURE FROM CONTROLLED FLIGHT Procedure.

items.title: Instrument scan patterns
items.lede: The concept of attitude flying is based upon the fact that a specific power setting when combined with a specific attitude will result in a specific aircraft performance. Once PAT is accomplished, scan to maintain the desired performance. Scan is the systematic process of monitoring the crosscheck and performance instruments to detect deviation from desired flight parameters, then applying the proper controls to make an appropriate timely correction. The goal is early error detection and correction.

items.title: Integrated (VMC) scan
items.lede: In introducing the basic flight maneuvers, the integrated flight instruction method will be used. This means that each flight maneuver will be performed by using both outside visual references and the flight instruments. The task of scanning in contact flying involves division of attention between the external and internal environment, setting attitudes with the nose and wings in relation to the horizon, and cross-checking them against the instruments in the cockpit.

items.title: Intentional spin entry
items.lede: Two primary factors must be present for an aircraft to spin: stalled AOA and yaw, rotation about the vertical axis. The spin entry is straightforward and procedural; the spin entry is not a finesse maneuver. It requires full back stick with ailerons neutral, fully deflected rudder, and PCL to idle. Practice spins to the left and right.

items.title: Intersections
items.lede: An intersection is a navigational fix that can be defined in the T-6B using VOR/DME, VOR only, the intersection of two or more radials from two or more NAVAIDs, or GPS. Intersections are used to identify significant points along departure procedures, airways, arrivals, holding areas, approach procedures, and missed approaches. When referencing two or more NAVAIDs, the primary NAVAID is the one used to navigate a track to the intersection, and a secondary NAVAID is one that provides a crosscut to identify the intersection along the primary track.

items.title: Inverted spin

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight

items.lede: Intentional inverted departures and spins are prohibited. In the inverted spins tested, high engine torque is the primary impetus which drives the aircraft into, and sustains, the inverted spin. When using the inverted spin recovery, the aircraft recovers within a half turn after the controls are applied. Power-on and inverted departures or spins will result in high loads on the engine and torque shaft.

items.title: Jet log

references.loc: Ch. 4 §7 — SNA Navigation Mission Planning Requirements

items.lede: Complete a Jet Log for all events required in the syllabus notes section of the Joint Primary Pilot Training (JPPT) master curriculum guide (a copy should be made for the instructor as well).

items.title: Knock-it-off
items.lede: Knock-it-off is a radio call used by a flight member to alert the formation to cease maneuvering. It is used when safety of flight is an issue, such as an emergency, a traffic threat, or a crewmember who has G-locked due to poor Anti-G Straining Maneuver execution during Tail Chase. This radio call should be preserved as an "unexpected stop and attention getter" and may be initiated by any flight member.

items.title: Landing flap landings
items.lede: Make a descending 180° balanced turn to final in the flaps LDG configuration. Upon reaching the 180, commence the approach turn by simultaneously lowering the nose to the 110 KIAS approach attitude and smoothly turning toward the 90.

items.title: Landing gear emergency extension
items.lede: Do not use the Landing Gear Emergency Extension checklist unless directed by the Landing Gear Malfunction, Hydraulic System Malfunctions, Battery Bus Inoperative, or the Battery and Generator Failure checklists.

items.title: Landing gear inspection

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Landing with Unsafe Gear Indications

items.lede: The aircraft with an unsafe gear indication should climb to an emergency orbit or delta pattern in accordance with local SOP or Course Rules, and coordinate with the Wingman to get an airborne landing gear inspection. The inspection should be conducted at a minimum of 2000 feet AGL. At no time shall student solos join-up to inspect landing gear.

items.title: Landing irregularities
items.lede: A deviation from a normal landing which could cause a dangerous situation to quickly develop. Airspeed in the flare is only slightly above stall airspeed, and even at slow airspeeds the elevator is still very effective, so an abrupt change in pitch could result in a balloon, a bounce, or even a stall.

items.title: Landing pattern stalls

events.title: Familiarization
events.label: Landing pattern (approach turn and landing attitude) stalls

items.lede: Proper recognition of and recovery from approach-to-stall conditions in the landing pattern. Training emphasis is on recognition of approach-to-stall indications and appropriate recovery procedures. Recover at first indication of stall, airframe buffet or stick shaker, whichever occurs first. Do not enter a full stall.
terms: Landing pattern (approach turn and landing attitude) stalls

items.title: Landing pattern
items.lede: The landing pattern is a geometric racetrack-shaped course flown so that an approach and landing may be executed in a systematic sequence. The landing line, the upwind leg, and the parallel Downwind leg form the sides of the racetrack pattern. These lines are joined together by the Crosswind turn and by the approach turn at the Downwind end of the pattern. The landing pattern is subdivided into three parts: the pattern, approach, and landing.

items.title: Lead, lag and pure pursuit

events.title: Formation
events.label: Principles of lead, lag and pure pursuit

items.lede: The concept of pursuit geometry between aircraft is fundamental to formation maneuvering. This geometry relates specifically to flight paths and planes of motion. Assuming both aircraft are moving forward at the same speed and in the same plane of motion, aircraft nose position relative to the other aircraft will determine the type of pursuit. There are three basic types of pursuit: lead, pure and lag.
terms: Principles of lead, lag and pure pursuit

items.title: Level speed change
items.lede: Level Speed Changes are taught to familiarize you with the various trim adjustments required with changes in airspeed, power setting, and aircraft configuration. The sequence is flown from normal cruise, 200 KIAS, to the no flap configuration, 120 KIAS, to the landing flap configuration, 120 KIAS, and then to normal cruise, 200 KIAS.

items.title: Local area departure
items.lede: Inform Navy Corpus Ground of departure intentions when calling for taxi, requesting Taxi "VFR" for a Beach Line departure and every other Departure Procedure by name. Climb at 180 KIAS with no turn prior to 300' AGL, level off at 200 KIAS, and transit at 240 KIAS once clear of Class D airspace. When directed, contact Corpus Departure CH 8 UHF and state intentions on initial contact.

items.title: Local area flight procedures

references.loc: Ch. 1 §9 — Bird Aircraft Strike Hazard (BASH) Program
Ch. 2 §6 — Touchdown at Non-Tower Controlled Airfields

items.lede: The local flying area is the airspace within the continental United States, within a 125 nautical mile radius of KNGP, Texas, and offshore training areas, excluding the area within a 50 nautical mile radius of San Antonio VORTAC. All training flights must be conducted in strict compliance with the applicable weather sections of the wing instruction and applicable references, and all flights must plan to recover no later than 2359.

items.title: Local cross-country SOP

references.loc: Ch. 1 §7 — Cross Country and Special Procedures

items.lede: A cross-country flight is defined as a flight operating outside the local flying area or remaining overnight at an enroute destination airfield outside the Corpus Christi local area.

items.title: Local night VNAV SOP
items.lede: Aircraft must not operate within a SIGMET or Convective SIGMET at night unless they have an operable radar installed capable of detection and avoidance of isolated thunderstorms. Aerobatics, short breaks, formation and stalls are prohibited at night.

items.title: Local VFR sectional review
items.lede: During the Navigation stage of instruction, the VFR Sectional Aeronautical Chart with a scale of 1:500,000 will be used. The chart does not represent a true picture of the real world, but rather is a schematic diagram of certain characteristics of the world: a simplified, generalized, and codified presentation of a selected sample of some characteristics of the earth's surface, annotated with various names, numbers, boundaries, and reference grids. You must be completely familiar with every symbol contained on the chart.

items.title: Localizer approach
items.lede: A localizer approach is a non-precision approach that utilizes the localizer component of the ILS system to provide accurate course guidance to the runway centerline. The process of establishing the aircraft onto the FAC and localizer characteristics are exactly the same as those discussed for the ILS approach. Once established on the final approach course, the procedures closely reflect those used for other non-precision approaches. On approaches titled ILS or LOC, where the glideslope information is not used, or is unavailable, non-precision rules and minimums apply.

items.title: Loop
items.lede: The Loop is a 360° turn in the vertical plane with constant heading and nose track. Because it is executed in a single plane, the elevator is the principal control surface. Ailerons and rudder are used to maintain directional control and coordinated flight. The maneuver is complete when wings are level at the horizon on the same heading as at entry.

items.title: Loss of START READY light during start sequence

events.title: Familiarization Cockpit Procedures
events.label: Loss of start ready light during start sequence

items.lede: The engine start should be aborted manually if the PCL is moved or the ST READY green advisory message extinguishes during the start sequence. During a normal (auto) start, the PMU continuously monitors N1, ITT, and fuel flow.
terms: Loss of START READY light during start sequence

items.title: Lost aircraft procedures
items.lede: If you get lost, admit it and try to communicate using all available channels and navigation aids including the nearest function on the Flight Management System (FMS). Land at a suitable airfield before you run out of gas. Every situation will be different; therefore, it is impossible to establish a criterion that will apply to every set of circumstances. However, the following items, known as the five Cs will generally apply: **CONFESS, CLIMB, CONSERVE, COMMUNICATE, and COMPLY**.

items.title: Lost communication procedures
items.lede: Radio failure in a formation is a potentially confusing and hazardous situation. If NORDO (No Radio), all radios have failed. The formation should maintain VMC if able. The lead position should be offered to the NORDO aircraft in order to troubleshoot and attempt to re-establish radio communications. If radio contact cannot be re-established, the aircraft with the good radios shall take the Lead position to return to base.

items.title: Lost communications
items.lede: During two-way radio communications failure, when confronted with a situation not covered in the regulation, pilots are expected to exercise good judgment in whatever action they elect to take. The transponder should be adjusted to reply on Mode 3/A, Code 7600. If able to maintain flight in VMC continue flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable and notify ATC. If VMC is not encountered, continue the flight according to the route, altitude and leave clearance limit rules. The KNGP IFG prints four lost communications procedures for NAS Corpus Christi: after takeoff, on a local coded flight plan, in the GCA pattern, and on GCA final.

items.title: Lost sight procedures
items.lede: Lost sight is the term used by the Wingman to communicate that they have lost visual contact with the Lead aircraft during IMC conditions. During IMC formation flight, Wing will have very little reference to attitude, as their scan should be nearly solely on Lead's aircraft. If Wing loses sight of Lead, it may take Wing several seconds to transition to an effective instrument scan and transmit the "lost sight" radio call. For this reason, a smooth reduction of power once lost sight conditions are recognized is essential to reduce the likelihood of a mid-air.

items.title: Low fuel pressure
items.lede: If engine fuel feed pressure drops below 10 psi, and the boost pump fails to engage automatically, the FUEL PX warning will illuminate. If engine fuel feed pressure is fluctuating at or below 10 psi, the boost pump will alternately cycle on and off, illuminating and extinguishing the BOOST PUMP advisory.

items.title: Maneuvering speeds

numbers.label: VMO, at or below 19,020 feet MSL

references.loc: Ch. 5 — Maximum Operating Airspeed/Maximum Operating Mach Number (VMO/MMO)
Ch. 5 — Turbulent Air Penetration Speed Limitations (VG)

items.lede: NATOPS Chapter 5 publishes the airspeed limitations: operating maneuvering speed (VO), maximum operating airspeed and Mach number (VMO/MMO), the maximums with the flaps or the landing gear extended, and turbulent air penetration speed (VG). VO is 227 KIAS.

items.title: Memorized checklists

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: Most checklists are not performed from memory; however, the following checklists performed during critical phases of flight must be performed from memory: Lineup, After Takeoff, Operations, and Before Landing.

items.title: Minimum fuel requirements

numbers.label: Solo, depart KNGT or K4 MOA

items.lede: Aircraft shall carry fuel to fly from takeoff to the destination airfield, plus a reserve of 10 percent of the planned fuel requirement. In no case shall the planned fuel reserve after the final landing be less than 20 minutes of flight.

items.title: Missed approach
items.lede: A missed approach is a procedure used to discontinue an instrument approach if the runway environment is not in sight, or the aircraft is not in a position to make a safe landing. The primary concern if unable to land is to climb to a safe altitude. Therefore, establishing and maintaining a positive rate of climb should be your first priority if a missed approach is commenced. Your second priority should be to turn the aircraft, if required, to intercept the missed approach course or to the designated heading.

items.title: NATOPS limitations

numbers.label: Max rate of descent at touchdown
numbers.value: 600 feet per minute, normal tire pressure

numbers.label: Max rate of descent at touchdown
numbers.value: 780 feet per minute, maximum tire pressure

numbers.label: No canopy open on the ground above

references.loc: Ch. 5 — Taxi, Takeoff, and Landing Limitations

items.lede: Operating limitations include limitations that must be observed for safe operation of the aircraft and engine. The pilot will make all necessary entries in appropriate maintenance records to indicate when any limitations have been exceeded, including the time interval, where applicable, and the actual instrument reading of the limitation that was exceeded.

items.title: Night cockpit setup
items.lede: All instruments, control panels, and displays in both cockpits are lighted for operation during night or reduced light conditions. The NIGHT position is intended for use during night and low light operation, and if NIGHT mode is selected in either cockpit, the MFDs and UFCPs in the whole aircraft are placed into the night mode.

items.title: Night emergency procedures
items.lede: Comply with the NATOPS Flight Manual. If the engine fails at or above 2000 feet AGL, a restart is not attempted or unsuccessful, and a lighted runway is not immediately available, ejection is highly recommended. If the engine fails below 2000 feet AGL, attempting a restart is not recommended.

items.title: Night flying considerations
items.lede: Good night flying, like good night driving, requires increased care. You will have to identify obstructions and other aircraft by such small identifying features as a few colored lights. The eye uses different parts for night vision than for day vision, spatial disorientation is often experienced at night from lack of a well-defined horizon, and distance and relative motion are judged by the distance between two lights on the same aircraft.

items.title: Night VFR chart interpretation
items.lede: Obstructions are marked and lighted to warn pilots of their presence during daytime and nighttime conditions. Most have aviation red obstruction lights. Obstructions with high intensity flashing white lights are depicted with an obstruction symbol with lightning bolts coming from the top.

items.title: Night VNAV timing and course corrections

events.title: Night Navigation
events.label: Night VNAV timing and course corrections

items.lede: Timing corrections use, in order, the proportional method, the ten percent method, and off-course maneuvering; course corrections use a feature on your route, flown to with the Flight Path Marker in the HUD, then funneling features between 10 and 2 o'clock, then a Standard Closing Angle. During Night VNAV, where most useful references will be lighted, the Wingtip Method gives your distance from a reference as you pass abeam it. When flying a visual navigation route under VFR, visibility and cloud clearance requirements are different in controlled and uncontrolled airspace.
terms: Night VNAV timing and course corrections

items.title: No-flap landings
items.lede: Make a descending 180° balanced turn to final in the flaps Up configuration. A flap-up landing will not require a transition, a PCL reduction, until the 180. Upon reaching the 180, commence the approach turn by simultaneously lowering the nose to the 120 KIAS approach attitude and smoothly turning toward the 90.

items.title: No-gyro approach

references.loc: §5.3.5.5 — Final Approach Abnormalities During Radar Approaches

items.lede: A no-gyro approach is available to a pilot under radar control who experiences circumstances wherein the directional gyro or other stabilized compass is inoperative or inaccurate. When this occurs, the pilot should so advise ATC and request a no-gyro vector or approach.

items.title: No start
items.lede: In the AUTO start mode, if a no start is detected, the PMU should terminate the start sequence. The engine start should be aborted manually if no rise of ITT is evident within 10 seconds after fuel flow indications.

items.title: No-wind orbit
items.lede: The second passage of the holding fix commences the no-wind orbit. A no-wind orbit is used to determine the general wind direction and any heading and timing adjustments that will be needed to offset their effects.

items.title: Non-radar environment communications

references.loc: §C117 — Additional Mandatory Reports for Non-Radar Environment

items.lede: Federal Aviation Regulations require pilots to maintain a listening watch on the appropriate frequency and to furnish position reports passing certain reporting points. Reporting points are indicated by symbol on enroute charts: the designated compulsory reporting point symbol is the solid triangle and the on request reporting point symbol is an open triangle. Reports passing an on request reporting point are only necessary when requested by ATC.

items.title: Normal takeoff
items.lede: Takeoff is the movement of the aircraft from its starting point on the runway until it leaves the ground in controlled flight. Although a relatively simple maneuver, the takeoff presents numerous potential hazards: the dynamics of high engine thrust, possible directional control problems, the potential for runway incursions, high-speed aborts and low-altitude engine failures make the takeoff regime of flight unique in its safety challenges. Although the takeoff and climb process is one continuous maneuver, it is divided into three separate steps for purposes of explanation: takeoff roll, rotation, and initial climb.

items.title: NOTAMs

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: NOTAM to include local, FDC, center, special notices, International/Domestic Notices, and GPS

references.loc: §1.3.4 — DOD Flight Information Publications (FLIPs) and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs)

items.lede: A notice to airmen (NOTAM) is a notice containing information (not known sufficiently in advance to publicize by other means) concerning the establishment, condition, or change in any component (facility, service, or procedure of, or hazard in the National Airspace System) the timely knowledge of which is essential to personnel concerned with flight operations. NOTAM information is classified as Domestic NOTAMs (NOTAM D), Flight Data Center (FDC) NOTAMs, International NOTAMs, or Military NOTAMs.
terms: NOTAM to include local, FDC, center, special notices, International/Domestic Notices, and GPS

items.title: OBOGS and pressurization system
items.lede: The OBOGS provides each pilot with an automatically regulated oxygen supply which has a slight positive pressure and no duration limitations. Oxygen is extracted from conditioned bleed air by pressure swing adsorption using a molecular sieve. The pressurization system maintains an 8000-foot cockpit altitude until a differential pressure of 3.6 ± 0.2 psi is reached at 18,069 feet.

items.title: OBOGS FAIL message
items.lede: Illumination of the OBOGS FAIL message is a positive indication of a system malfunction. Failure of the OBOGS system may be accompanied by reduced pressure and/or quantity of breathing gas and may result in hypoxia symptoms if corrective action is not taken immediately.

items.title: OBOGS malfunctions
items.lede: Illumination of the OBOGS FAIL message is a positive indication of a system malfunction. Failure of the OBOGS system may be accompanied by reduced pressure and/or quantity of breathing gas and may result in hypoxia symptoms if corrective action is not taken immediately. If physiological symptoms are recognized at any point, proceed immediately to the OBOGS FAILURE/OVERTEMP/PHYSIOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS Checklist.

items.title: Obstacle departure procedures
items.lede: Obstacle departure procedures provide obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the appropriate enroute structure. Found in DOD FLIP approach plates, ODPs will be labeled with the word OBSTACLE in the title.

items.title: Oil and propeller systems
items.lede: The oil system has a capacity of 18.5 U.S. quarts and provides a constant supply of filtered oil to the engine bearings, reduction gears, accessory drives, and propeller throughout normal and aerobatic flight maneuvers. The engine power management unit (PMU) controls the propeller RPM by varying the propeller blade angle with oil pressure through the propeller interface unit (PIU). Pressurized engine oil forces the piston forward to decrease pitch toward fine. When oil pressure against the piston is reduced, the blades turn toward coarse pitch.

items.title: Oil system malfunction or low oil pressure

events.title: Familiarization Emergency Procedures Trainer
events.label: Oil system malfunction or low oil pressure

Check OIL TRX circuit breaker if oil pressure below

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Oil System Malfunction or Low Oil Pressure

items.lede: The SCU activates the red OIL PX warning if oil pressure drops to 40 psi or below when above idle power, or when oil pressure drops to 15 psi or below at idle power. Additionally, the SCU illuminates the amber OIL PX caution whenever sensed oil pressure is between 15 and 40 psi at idle power, and if the oil pressure drops to between 40 and 90 psi, for 10 seconds, above idle power.
terms: Oil system malfunction or low oil pressure

items.title: OLF arrival and departure
items.lede: The outlying field entry is a series of uniform procedures by which aircraft enter the landing pattern, and the outlying field departure is a series of uniform procedures by which aircraft depart the pattern. Since numerous aircraft may be using the same outlying field simultaneously, it is absolutely necessary that each aircraft conform to the same systematic pattern and standard operating procedures for safety and efficiency. Goliad is the primary outlying field for TW-4 T-6 aircraft. Entry is via a 4 NM initial point on extended runway centerline, and departure is from upwind at 800' MSL turning approximately 45 degrees away from runway heading.

items.title: OLF course rules

events.title: RDO Pattern Party
events.label: OLF Course rules for field of use

events.title: RDO Pattern Party
events.label: OLF Course rules for field of use

items.lede: Goliad is the primary outlying field for TW-4 T-6 aircraft. It is a lighted airport for day VFR touch and go and emergency landing pattern practice. The field is open for touch and go operations provided a qualified Runway Duty Officer (RDO) and Crash Crew are in place; low approaches are permitted without a RDO on station. Traffic patterns are depicted on Plate 2-13, advisory radio calls must be made per the instruction, and no clearance to land will be issued by the RDO.
terms: OLF Course rules for field of use

items.title: OLF/RDO communication
items.lede: Two-way radio communication with the RDO or crash crew is required for entry into the traffic pattern at an outlying field. Advisory radio calls must be made per the Course Rules Manual, and no clearance to land will be issued by the RDO. Aircraft are responsible for ensuring proper interval for their break. Once in the break, an aircraft is considered established in the pattern and only the aircraft ID number is required when making radio calls.

items.title: On-speed crosscheck in crosswind conditions

numbers.label: Gust additive
numbers.value: ½ gust factor, up to 10 knots

items.lede: At no time during the approach turn should you slow below on speed AOA (amber donut AOA indication). Approach AOA (amber donut) continues to provide the optimum approach speed and maneuver speed (regardless of bank angle). The corresponding indicated airspeed at amber donut as read from the PFD will be different based on aircraft weight and angle of bank.

items.title: Out-of-control flight

events.title: Familiarization
events.label: OCF recovery and airborne damaged aircraft

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight

items.lede: A situation in which the aircraft does not respond immediately and in a normal sense to application of flight controls is considered out-of-control flight (OCF) or a departure. It is possible to depart controlled flight as a result of improper or overly aggressive control inputs near stall, mechanical failures, atmospheric conditions, or a combination thereof. In general, OCF can be divided into three categories: poststall gyrations, incipient spins, and steady-state spins. Recovery from inadvertent loss of aircraft control, including poststall gyrations and incipient spins, can be accomplished by promptly reducing power to IDLE, and positively neutralizing flight controls in all axes.
terms: OCF recovery and airborne damaged aircraft

items.title: Over-the-station intercepts

numbers.label: Turn to intercept if course change over

items.lede: An over-the-station intercept is a procedure used to intercept and fly outbound on a specific radial immediately after station passage. This procedure is appropriate during airways navigation and instrument approaches that use VOR facilities for enroute navigation, initial approach fixes, final approach fixes or missed approach procedures. Upon station passage, perform the 6 Ts as appropriate.

items.title: PAR approach

references.loc: §5.3.5.5 — Final Approach Abnormalities During Radar Approaches

items.lede: During a PAR approach, the controller utilizes an airport surveillance radar system to transition the aircraft to final and then hands off to another controller. This final controller utilizes a precision radar system located at the airport to provide precise course, range and glideslope feedback during the final approach segment. Because both course and glideslope information is available, it constitutes a precision approach.

items.title: PAR without glideslope

references.loc: §907 — Airport Surveillance Approach (ASR) and PAR Without Glideslope (PAR W/O GS)
§5.3.5.5 — Final Approach Abnormalities During Radar Approaches

items.lede: Because glideslope information is either not available or not used, the ASR and PAR W/O GS approaches are both non-precision, and both are accomplished using the same procedures. The PAR W/O GS uses the ASR to establish the aircraft on final and then hands the aircraft off to a final controller who utilizes only the azimuth portion of the precision radar to provide course and range information. Due to the increased accuracy of course and range information available during the PAR W/O GS, the associated MDA may be lower.

items.title: Parade sequence checkpoints
items.lede: Once the flight is established in the area and Ops Checks are complete, begin the parade sequence. The parade sequence is a series of tasks which allow both students the opportunity to practice flying basic formation positions and maneuvers. Parade Position is a fixed position on the left/right 45º bearing from Lead with sufficient wingtip clearance and step-down. The perfect Parade Position is transitory, and every correction has a corresponding re-correction to ensure Altitude (step-down), Bearing line, and Closure/Separation (the A-B-Cs) are correct.

items.title: Pattern adjustments for crosswinds
items.lede: Compensate for crosswinds in the landing pattern to maintain the normal ground track. All pilots should be able to assess crosswinds and understand how they affect pattern operations. The proper application of crosswind controls is essential to executing landings.

items.title: PCL cutoff and inadvertent engine shutdown

events.title: Familiarization Flight 0
events.label: PCL cutoff and inadvertent engine shutdown

items.lede: The PCL incorporates a cutoff gate to prevent inadvertent engine shutdown. Mishaps have occurred due to inadvertent lifting of PCL idle cutoff gate during flight.
terms: PCL cutoff and inadvertent engine shutdown

items.title: PEL from the pattern

references.loc: §705 — Precautionary Emergency Landing from the Pattern

items.lede: Use PEL procedures if indications of an impending engine failure occur while in the landing pattern. The same indications of an impending engine failure as discussed in the PEL may occur in the landing pattern. This maneuver affords the opportunity to practice intercepting the ELP at or before low key while already established in the landing pattern.

items.lede: Three airstart procedures are approved for this aircraft: PMU NORM; PMU OFF; and Immediate Airstart (PMU NORM). The PMU NORM airstart procedure will provide the least complicated airstart. Refer to PMU OFF airstart if PMU FAIL message is present.

items.lede: Three airstart procedures are approved for this aircraft: PMU NORM; PMU OFF; and Immediate Airstart (PMU NORM). If the PMU has malfunctioned (PMU FAIL warning illuminated), conduct the airstart with the PMU off. With the PMU off, the igniters will not automatically activate and must be selected manually.

items.title: Point-to-point
items.lede: If a NAVAID (station) transmits both radial and DME information and the aircraft equipment is capable of processing that information, it can be used to navigate from present position to a specific RADIAL and DME from that station via the most direct path. If cleared direct to a RADIAL/DME fix, the pilot may be radar vectored or employ Point to Point (PTP) navigation. For PTP navigation, the turn to an initial heading should be initiated as soon as possible once cleared.

items.title: Power-off stall
items.lede: Stall the aircraft in a power-off condition to demonstrate the proper recovery when no power is available. Power-off stalls are flown to practice recovery from potentially dangerous low airspeed conditions prior to high key and during the ELP. Airspeed may decrease for various reasons, including inattention, task saturation, and attempts to stretch the glide to regain profile.

items.title: Power-on stalls
items.lede: Stall the aircraft in a power-on condition to demonstrate the proper recovery when power is available. Aircraft pitch and bank angle will be held constant until un-commanded nose drop and/or unplanned rolling motion. An entry speed of 150 KIAS results in about 1500 to 2000 feet altitude gain.

items.title: Precautionary emergency landing

Level deceleration, per 10 knots above 125 KIAS

references.loc: Ch. 2 §4 — Flights Following Precautionary Emergency Landing (PEL) or Emergency Landing
§3.2 — Actual Emergencies and Precautionary Emergency Landings (PELs)

items.lede: The PEL procedure should be executed whenever indications of a possible engine failure exist and/or when directed by the checklist. Use power, airspeed, altitude, and configuration to intercept and maintain the emergency landing pattern profile.

items.lede: Familiarization maneuvers briefed on earlier events, any of which may be discussed on this event.

items.lede: The discuss items already briefed in the stage, any of which can be asked. The list below is built from the syllabus.

events.title: Day Familiarization

items.lede: Maneuvers briefed on earlier events, any of which may be discussed on this event.
terms: Any previously discussed maneuver or procedure

items.title: Procedure turn approach
items.lede: Reverse the aircraft heading within assigned airspace in order to align it with the final approach course. The procedure turn approach is an instrument maneuver used to reverse direction and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course while insuring the remain within distance is observed. Procedure turns are depicted by a barb symbol on the approach plate, and the barb indicates which side of the outbound course to complete the turn.

items.title: Progressive spin
items.lede: A progressive spin is a result of misapplication of recovery controls. Reversing the rudder direction during a steady state spin while maintaining full aft stick will result in a spin in the opposite direction.

items.title: Radial-arc intercepts
items.lede: On some approaches, missed approaches and departure procedures, you will be required to transition from a radial onto an arc. In these situations a lead point will be calculated to determine when to start your turn off of the radial onto the arc.

items.title: Radial intercept procedures
items.lede: A radial intercept is a procedure used to position the aircraft on a nearby radial with a new course inbound or outbound when not over the station. Radial intercepts are performed in training to practice orientation around a NAVAID, and may be used when navigating on airways and during some instrument approaches. The objective is to establish an intercept heading that will result in an appropriate angle and rate of intercept to the new radial or course.

items.title: Radial rendezvous
items.lede: A Blind Rendezvous, referred to as a TACAN rendezvous in fleet aircraft, is a visual circular rendezvous employed to rendezvous a flight above the weather after takeoff, or during the mission if the flight is separated. It is normally executed in a left-hand turn tangent to the briefed fix at a specified airspeed, altitude, and direction, inbound or outbound. The fix will be a VFR ground reference, an FMS reference point, or a radial/DME fix.

items.title: Rate of descent calculation

references.loc: Appendix B — 60-to-1 Rule and Other Formulas
Ch. 4 — Descent Rates and Glidepaths for Nonprecision Approaches

items.lede: NM/Min x Ft/NM = Rate of Climb/Descent in Feet per minute (FPM), and NM/Min x 100 ft x Gradient = Required VSI. To determine the required rate of descent on a non-precision approach, subtract the TDZE from the FAF altitude and divide this by the time inbound.

items.title: Recommended altitudes

references.loc: §907 — Airport Surveillance Approach (ASR) and PAR Without Glideslope (PAR W/O GS)

items.lede: If requested by the pilot, recommended altitudes will be issued at each mile, based on the descent gradient established for the procedure, down to the last mile that is at or above the MDA. They are available on the ASR and PAR without glideslope approaches, both of which are non-precision.

items.title: Route management
items.lede: The primary means of navigation used on Visual Navigation flights will be a combination of Dead Reckoning (DR) and pilotage. DR is a logical system in which time, velocity, and distance are combined to arrive at a position. Pilotage is flying by visual reference to features on the ground.

items.title: Runaway trim
items.lede: Whenever the trim interrupt button is being depressed, or when the trim disconnect switch is set to disconnect, all trim systems are disengaged and the TAD is disconnected. Illumination of the TAD FAIL caution indicates that the TAD has failed. Loss of the TAD increases pilot workload but has no other effect on mission capability.

items.title: RVFAC for RNAV approaches

references.loc: Ch. 1 — Vectoring to Final Approach Fix (FAF)

items.lede: Air traffic control clearance to the FAF can be handled by converting the loaded approach into a straight-in approach. This is accomplished by direct-to navigation to intercept the inbound course to the FAF.

items.title: Radar vectors to final approach course

references.loc: §820 — Radar Vectors to Final Approach Course (RVFAC)

items.lede: Radar vectors to final approach course is a procedure used by approach control to increase the arrival rate of aircraft by providing vectors onto the final approach course through the most expeditious routes consistent with traffic situations. Although this routing does expedite arrival at your destination, it has one characteristic of which you should be aware: the lack of published minimum altitudes until joining a segment of a published approach.
terms: Radar vectors to final approach course

items.title: S-1 pattern
items.lede: Maintain heading and airspeed throughout a series of constant rate descents and climbs. This pattern is flown at 150 KIAS and on any numbered or cardinal heading. It consists of a timed 1000 FPM descent for 1000 feet, followed by a timed 1000 FPM climb for 1000 feet. This series, descent and climb, is performed twice.

items.title: Safety check and call

events.title: Familiarization Cockpit Procedures
events.label: Safety check/call prior to cockpit entry and departing aircraft

references.loc: §2 — How to Use This Checklist Guide

items.lede: Respect the Seat. Ejection seat and canopy fracturing system safety is paramount during ground operations, and if unintentionally or improperly fired the results could be fatal. Never enter or exit the airplane without the ejection seat safety pins installed.
terms: Safety check/call prior to cockpit entry and departing aircraft

items.title: SCATSAFE maneuver
items.lede: The SCATSAFE maneuver is designed to demonstrate various performance characteristics of the aircraft when in a near-stalled condition. This maneuver will be demonstrated by the instructor. Every takeoff and landing you make requires you to operate the aircraft at low airspeed.

items.title: Scheduling

references.loc: Ch. 1 §6 — Crew Day and Crew Rest
§2.1 — Crew Day / Crew Rest / Work Week Limitations

items.lede: Crew day begins with the first scheduled event or official duty at VT-27, and at VT-28 when aircrew arrive at the squadron base location or at their appointed place of duty. SNA crew day ends upon completion of the last scheduled syllabus event, to include associated debrief and paperwork, and crew rest follows it. VT-27 and VT-28 each publish their own limits on crew day and crew rest, and on what may be scheduled in a day.

items.title: Seat height and rudder pedal adjustment

events.title: CNAF M-3710.7 Level-A Mission Readiness Training
events.label: Seat height and rudder pedal adjustment

events.title: Familiarization Flight 0
events.label: Seat height and rudder pedal adjustment

items.lede: Seat height and rudder pedals are adjusted at consecutive items of the Interior Inspection checklist. Seat height is adjusted so that it allows a clear view of the HUD, instrument panel, and master warning/caution annunciators.
terms: Seat height and rudder pedal adjustment

items.title: Section approach procedures
items.lede: The Section Approach is used to expedite the recovery or for mutual support during certain emergencies. The key to a good formation approach is for Lead to fly a smooth, accurate instrument or visual approach, and for Wing to be proactive about maintaining position and complying with signals. Wing should also be prepared to assume the responsibilities of Lead at any time.

items.title: Section PEL
items.lede: If the Lead aircraft experiences an emergency, a radio call should be made quickly to allow Wing to get separation in order to allow Lead to maneuver as needed. The new Wing will transition to the Perch Position, assist in clearing the flight path, and monitor the PEL aircraft's performance.

items.title: Section takeoff
items.lede: The section takeoff has many practical advantages. It is frequently used to expedite departures and alleviates the necessity for a rendezvous in poor weather conditions. Wing will fly formation from brake release to rotation and into the airborne phase. Early detection and correction for changes in relative motion are the keys to performing a good section takeoff.

items.title: Securing the rear cockpit for solo
items.lede: The rear cockpit is secured for solo flight under Interior Inspection. When flying solo, the ISS mode selector shall be set to SOLO. Failure to secure rear cockpit for solo flight may result in restriction of flight control movement, and failure to secure the rear seat oxygen regulator will result in the loss of ability to deactivate OBOGS from the front seat. For solo flight, the aft UFCP LGT NIGHT/DAY/AUTO HUD switch should be set to DAY mode.
terms: Securing the rear cockpit for solo

items.title: See and avoid principle
items.lede: Simply stated, the "See and Avoid" Doctrine is a pilot's best defense against a midair collision. The causal factor most often noted in aircraft accident reports involving midair collisions is failure of the pilot to see and avoid the other aircraft. In most cases, at least one of the pilots involved could have seen the other in time to avoid contact if they had been using their eyes properly.

items.title: Shuttle descent
items.lede: A shuttle descent is a procedure used in holding to position the aircraft at a lower altitude. Descents in holding are normally initiated by ATC. If several aircraft are in holding at the same fix, they will be placed in a stack with a minimum altitude separation of 1000 feet. Shuttles will be used to descend each aircraft to the next lower stack altitude after the bottom aircraft in the stack has commenced the approach.

items.title: Slip
items.lede: A slip is an out-of-balance flight condition used to increase the sink rate and lose excess altitude while maintaining a constant airspeed and a specific track over the ground.

items.title: Slow flight
items.lede: The Slow Flight Maneuver is designed to develop your ability to fly the aircraft in a near-stalled condition. Every takeoff and landing you make requires you to operate the aircraft at low airspeed. During training, students are taught flight at minimum controllable airspeed so they may learn the effect that airspeed has on aircraft performance and controllability.

items.title: Smoke and fume elimination

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Smoke and Fume Elimination/Electrical Fire

items.lede: This procedure may be used in the event of smoke or fumes as a result of an electrical fire or contamination from the ECS system.

items.title: Snivels
items.lede: All aircrew shall check the flight schedule daily and notify the ODO as soon as possible in the event of a schedule conflict. Snivels are submitted in T-SHARP by 2359, SNAs seven business days prior to when the requested snivel is to occur and IPs two business days prior.

items.title: Speed brake use as a section

events.title: Formation
events.label: Speed brake use as a section

items.lede: During the recovery phase, Lead may elect to use the speed brake to increase descent rates or decelerate the formation. The speed brake is a drag device and is therefore less effective as the airspeed is reduced. Extending and retracting the speed brake will induce pitch changes that may need to be counteracted. It is imperative that Lead maintains a stable platform and is clear about the intended use of the speed brake to preclude any closure issues between Lead and Wing.
terms: Speed brake use as a section

items.title: Spin
items.lede: A spin requires stalled angle of attack simultaneously with sustained yaw rate. If either of these two conditions is absent, the aircraft will not enter a spin. The spin entry requires full back stick (ailerons neutral), fully deflected rudder, and PCL to idle. A spin progresses through three phases: post-stall gyrations, incipient spin, and steady state spin. The aircraft progresses from one phase to the next as long as pro-spin control inputs are applied.

items.title: Split-S
items.lede: The Split-S combines the first half of an Aileron Roll with the last half of a Loop. The aircraft climbs during entry and descends during recovery, and the maneuver is complete when the aircraft returns to level flight. It provides a means of rapidly converting the potential energy of altitude into airspeed while reversing the direction of flight.

items.title: Stabilized approach criteria

numbers.label: Circling, final segment
numbers.value: 500 feet above airport elevation or MDA, lower

references.loc: Ch. 4 — Descent Rates and Glidepaths for Nonprecision Approaches
§907 — Airport Surveillance Approach (ASR) and PAR Without Glideslope (PAR W/O GS)
§813 — Use of Radar Altimeter During Instrument Approaches

items.lede: Maintaining a constant approach speed, descent rate, vertical flight path, and configuration during the final stages of an approach is referred to as the stabilized approach concept. A stabilized approach is essential for safe turbojet operations and is also strongly recommended for propeller-driven airplanes and helicopters.

items.title: Standard course corrections
items.lede: Making in-flight corrections to course and time is simple; however, you must know how far off course you are before determining a correction. Making a correction without knowing your exact location typically results in greater error. The techniques, in order, are to identify a feature on your route and fly back to it, to use funneling features, and to use a Standard Closing Angle.

items.title: Standard instrument departure
items.lede: Standard instrument departures are air traffic control procedures printed in graphic form for pilot use. SIDs will provide obstruction clearance and a transition from the terminal area to the appropriate enroute structure and can be found in DOD FLIP approach plates.

items.title: Standard time corrections
items.lede: Timing corrections are simply a matter of changing your GS for a period of time or off-course maneuvering. Off-course maneuvering will change the distance you fly, which will affect your timing. The recommended methods are the proportional method, the ten percent method and off-course maneuvering.

items.title: Standard terminal arrival
items.lede: A Standard Terminal Arrival is an Air Traffic Control coded IFR arrival route established for application by arriving IFR aircraft destined for certain airports. RNAV STARs for arrivals serve the same purpose, but are only used by aircraft equipped with a Flight Management System. The purpose of both is to simplify clearance delivery procedures and facilitate transition between enroute and instrument approach procedures.

items.title: Station passage
items.lede: Station passage is defined as the moment the aircraft passes directly over or abeam the radio facility.

items.title: Steady-state spin recovery
items.lede: After completing approximately three turns, the spin will have entered a near steady-state condition. Recover from a steady state spin by using NATOPS erect spin recovery procedures.

items.title: Steep turns
items.lede: Maintain smooth, coordinated flight in turns to specific headings at steeper than normal bank angles. These turns will normally be practiced at 45 and 60 degrees of bank and 150 KIAS, but other airspeeds and angles of bank are permissible. Enter a steep turn in the same manner as a normal turn.

items.title: Stereo routes
items.lede: A stereo route is a routinely used route of flight established by users and ARTCC identified by a coded name. These routes simplify flight plan handling and communications.

items.title: Strange Field operations

references.loc: Ch. 1 §7 — Cross Country and Special Procedures

items.lede: If mission requirements dictate an overnight stay and ground support equipment or personnel are not available, the pilot-in-command will be responsible for postflight and preflight inspections of the aircraft. The AC/IP is responsible for the physical security of the aircraft, aircraft tie-downs, chocks, and hangar space as necessary. The AC must inventory the fuel packet and ensure proper completion of fuel receipts, to include printing and signing of the AC's name on all fuel receipts.

items.title: Strike of ground object

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground

items.lede: A prop strike is one of the conditions NATOPS lists for the Emergency Engine Shutdown On The Ground procedure, alongside an engine fire, a chip light, the aircraft appearing likely to depart the prepared surface, and any other serious ground emergency.

items.title: Tail chase

numbers.label: Floor
numbers.value: 500 feet above block bottom, if higher

items.lede: Through the use of lead, lag, and pure pursuit, students will further learn the basics of how flight paths relate to each other in the dynamic maneuvering of the Tail Chase. Tail Chase demonstrates the effects of lead and lag pursuit on nose-to-tail distance through the use of aerobatic maneuvering.

items.title: Takeoff and approach minimums

events.title: Radio Instruments
events.label: CNAF M-3710.7 takeoff and approach minimums

events.title: Instrument Navigation
events.label: CNAF M-3710.7 takeoff and approach minimums

references.loc: §5.3.5.4 — Criteria for Continuing Instrument Approaches to a Landing

items.lede: On a standard instrument rating, takeoff requires the published minimums for the available non-precision approach, but not less than 300-foot ceiling and 1-statute mile visibility, and where a precision approach compatible with installed and operable aircraft equipment is available, takeoff is authorized at that approach's minimums for the landing runway in use but in no case below 200-foot ceiling and 1/2-statute-mile visibility/2,400-foot RVR. Absolute minimums for a single-piloted fixed-wing aircraft executing an approach are 200-foot ceiling/height above touchdown and visibility of 1/2 statute-mile/2,400 feet RVR.
terms: CNAF M-3710.7 takeoff and approach minimums

items.title: Takeoff flap landings
items.lede: Make a descending 180° balanced turn to final in the flaps TO configuration. Upon reaching the 180, commence the approach turn by simultaneously lowering the nose to the 115 KIAS approach attitude and smoothly turning toward the 90.

items.title: Teardrop approach
items.lede: A teardrop approach makes use of an outbound to inbound radial intercept maneuver to reverse course and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course while insuring the remain within distance is observed. A non-depicted teardrop approach is an authorized variant to the procedure turn, and is flown by intercepting an outbound radial offset 20° to the protected barb side of the procedure turn final approach course.

items.title: Terminate
items.lede: Terminate is a radio call, normally initiated by the Flight Lead, to terminate an exercise or maneuvering. This differs from the knock-it-off call in that it is anticipated and expected, such as after cruise maneuvering. Wing will request, or Lead will direct, a terminate.

items.title: Three Cs
items.lede: Accomplish and/or review the Three Cs before performing stall maneuvers. They are Configuration, Checklist, and Clear Area. The Three Cs may be accomplished in any order and are not required between individual maneuvers if flown in a series.

items.title: Time on target
items.lede: Time on Target is the exact arrival time at the last checkpoint based upon the preplanned total route time. Meeting a TOT can mean the difference of mission success or mission failure when working with other military assets. In order to successfully make your TOT, prior planning will be required.

items.title: Timed turns
items.lede: A timed turn, maintaining a specific rate of turn in degrees per second, to an assigned heading maintaining altitude and airspeed. During normal IFR flight, turns will generally be performed at either standard or half standard rate. The Standard Rate Turn (SRT) is 3° per second, so a turn of 180° will take one minute and a 360° turn will take two minutes.

items.title: Tire failures

references.loc: Ch. 3 — Landing with Blown Main Tire

items.lede: It may not be obvious that a main tire is blown until well into the landing roll. First indications of a blown main tire may include a pull towards the failed tire, or a rumble or shudder which can be mistaken for nose wheel shimmy.

items.title: Tracking
items.lede: Tracking is the process of flying direct to a station or waypoint, correcting for winds, such that the aircraft track over the ground is the most direct route. Maintain heading equal to course until deviation is noted on the CDI and bearing pointer, determine the general direction of the wind, turn to re-intercept the desired course, then select a heading that will hold the aircraft on course.

items.title: Trim
items.lede: The secondary flight controls include electrically actuated pitch, roll and yaw trim systems and a rudder trim aid device (TAD). They are used for trimming and balancing the aircraft in flight and to reduce the force required to actuate the primary flight control surfaces. To trim, deflect the trim switch in the opposite direction as the applied flight control force until that force is relieved.

items.title: Trouble T
items.lede: An obstacle departure procedure that has been developed solely for obstacle avoidance will be indicated with the symbol T on IAP charts, departure procedure charts, ODP or standard instrument departure plates.

items.title: Turn pattern
items.lede: The Turn Pattern is a series of constant angle of bank turns while maintaining altitude and airspeed. It consists of two 30° angle of bank turns in opposite directions for 90° of heading change, two 45° angle of bank turns in opposite directions for 180° of heading change, and two 60° angle of bank turns in opposite directions for 360° of heading change.

items.title: UFCP failure

references.loc: Ch. 1 — Alternate Communication and Navigation System (ALT CNS) and Alternate Barometric (ALT BARO)

items.lede: In the event of a UFCP failure, all data entry capabilities are disabled from the failed unit. In the case of UFCP failure, pressing ALT CNS (R5) or ALT BARO (L5) allows pilots to access the FMS generated alternate controls.

items.title: Unauthorized solo maneuvers

references.loc: Ch. 1 §6 — Crew Day and Crew Rest

items.lede: Solos may not practice spins, stalls, simulated engine failures, PPELs, or any maneuver which has not been previously introduced.
