items.lede: This procedure should be used whenever uncommanded power changes occur or the engine fails to produce expected power. A loss of thrust caused by uncommanded propeller feathering may be the result of an errant electrical signal to the feather dump solenoid causing reduction in oil pressure to the propeller pitch control mechanism.

items.title: Uncontrolled field instrument communications

references.loc: Appendix C §C126 — Handoff to Tower or Advisory Frequency
§608 — Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers

items.lede: At an airport not served by a tower or FSS, the controller will approve a change to the advisory service frequency when they no longer require direct communications. If operating on an IFR flight plan to an airport where there is no functioning control tower, the pilot must initiate cancellation of the IFR flight plan.

items.title: Unintentional instrument flight
items.lede: Instrument conditions are to be avoided at all times while operating VFR in the Contact stage, and at all times during a solo. If actual instrument flight is encountered, maintain aircraft control, climb to the safe altitude if below it, and get out of IMC the way it was entered.

items.title: VFR chart preparation
items.lede: Select the charts to be used for the flight and check the dates of expiration to make certain they are current. A general rule when preparing your chart is to minimize marking up the chart to avoid possibly obscuring potential needed information. Recommend all marks be done initially in pencil to allow easy correction. Ballpoint black ink can be used after all work is completed and proofread.

items.title: VFR field entry/departure (AIM)

references.loc: §608 — Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers
§607 — Approach Control Service for VFR Arriving Aircraft

items.lede: When operating at an airport where traffic control is being exercised by a control tower, pilots are required to maintain two-way radio contact with the tower while operating within the Class B, Class C, or Class D surface area unless the tower authorizes otherwise. At airports without an operating control tower, a segmented circle visual indicator system, if installed, is designed to provide traffic pattern information. The key to communicating at an airport without an operating control tower is selection of the correct common frequency.

items.title: Visual descent point
items.lede: Depending on the location of the MAP, the descent from the MDA often will have to be initiated prior to reaching the MAP in order to execute a normal (approximately 3°) descent to landing. This point is called the Visual Descent Point (VDP). The VDP will often be published on the approach chart; if not depicted, it may be computed.

items.title: Visual signals
items.lede: Your visual or radio communications within the flight must be clear and timely to avoid confusion. The Wingman should have time to acknowledge the signal before Lead executes the maneuver. Visual signals will generally be given to Wing when in parade.

items.title: Visual straight-in
items.lede: A VFR straight-in approach may be used at either military or civil airfields when use of the "Break" (or "overhead" at civil fields) would be precluded or impractical due to weather, traffic, or local procedures. These type approaches may also be used in conjunction with certain emergencies (e.g., in-flight damage). Every straight-in approach will be different, depending on altitude and aircraft position relative to the runway. The pilot must use their judgment and experience to adjust the aircraft's flight path and/or configuration to safely and efficiently execute the approach and landing.

items.title: V-n diagram

references.loc: Ch. 5 — Maximum Operating Airspeed/Maximum Operating Mach Number (VMO/MMO)

items.lede: The operating flight strengths are shown in the Operating Flight Strength (Vn) Diagram, which plots load factor against indicated airspeed for a clean wing at 5633 pounds. It carries one envelope for sea level and one for 31,000 feet, bounded above and below by the symmetric and asymmetric maneuver limits and on the right by a limit speed.

items.title: VOR approach procedures
items.lede: Fly the final segment of the instrument approach on speed, on course and arrive at the published MDA prior to the MAP to set the aircraft up for landing. This segment of the approach is the most demanding, as the aircraft is slow, low, and configured.

items.title: Wave-off
items.lede: The wave-off is a set of standard procedures used to effect the safe discontinuation of an approach. A wave-off may be initiated by the pilot, or may be directed by an external source: RDO, wheels watch, wave-off lights, IP, tower, another aircraft. The reason for an externally directed wave-off may not be apparent to the pilot, but the wave-off is mandatory unless a greater emergency exists.

items.title: Weight and balance

references.loc: Ch. 5 — Center of Gravity Limitations (Landing Gear Extended)

items.lede: It is the pilot’s responsibility to operate the aircraft within the weight and balance limitations specified in Section V. Three options are available to determine if the aircraft configuration is under the weight limits and within the CG limits. Maximum ramp weight is 6950 pounds and maximum takeoff weight is 6900 pounds; the allowable aft CG limit at all weights is 26.0% MAC.

items.title: Wind shear recovery

numbers.label: Severe windshear
numbers.value: Vertical speed change greater than 500 feet per minute

numbers.label: Microburst downdrafts
numbers.value: In excess of 6000 feet per minute

numbers.label: Approach airspeed
numbers.value: Up to 10 knots faster than normal

references.loc: Ch. 7 — Landing with Wind Gradient or Windshear

items.lede: Windshear is a dramatic change of wind speed and/or direction over a short distance along the flight path. Severe windshear is that which produces airspeed changes greater than 15 knots or vertical speed changes greater than 500 feet per minute. If windshear is encountered during an approach for landing, execute a go around/waveoff.

items.title: Wingman/flight leader responsibilities
items.lede: The Designated Flight Lead is an administrative position, that in Primary is the instructor pilot designated on the flight schedule by the commanding officer. The Designated Flight Lead is the pilot who is ultimately responsible for the mission objectives and the safe and orderly conduct of the flight, and may fly in either position during the conduct of the flight. The Formation Lead is a physical position that may change throughout the flight: the pilot at the controls who is flying the lead position and is responsible for immediate conduct of the flight.

items.title: Wingover

numbers.label: Maximum bank at the reference point

items.lede: The Wingover is a 180° reversal in the direction of flight accomplished by combining a smooth climbing turn for 90° with a smooth diving turn for 90°. Recovery should be on the same altitude and approximately the same airspeed at which the maneuver was started. It is a slow and gentle maneuver when properly executed, and no abrupt control movements are necessary.
